title: Cairo Film Festival Pitching Platform Awards $410,000 to Arab Film Projects
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 23, 2026 1:01pm PT Cairo Film Festival Pitching Platform Awards $410,000 to Arab Film Projects Winners include ‘The Story of the Mountain’ and ‘Their Ghosts Never Left My Home’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest ‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’ 2 days ago ‘Your Daughter’ Director on Bonds With Mom, Marianne Khoury, and ‘Uncle Joe,’ Youssef Chahine: ‘Filmmaking Is Really About Healing’ 2 days ago ‘Four Minus Three’ Takes Cairo Film Festival’s Golden Pyramid, While ‘Summer Meadow’ Wins Three Awards and ‘The Day of Wrath’ Nabs Two 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "The Story of the Mountain" (Courtesy of Cairo Film Festival) The 12th Cairo Film Connection , the pitching platform of the Cairo Film Festival , handed out 53 awards worth a combined $410,000 to Arab film projects at the end of its industry sidebar, Cairo Industry Days . The awards included 17 cash grants, 31 in-kind awards and five invitations to international film markets and labs, marking a significant increase in support from previous editions. This year’s CFC brought together 17 projects from 12 countries, spanning fiction and documentary films in development and post-production. The platform hosted 104 one-on-one meetings between filmmakers and regional and international industry representatives. Related Stories India's T-Series and Hungama Launch Microdrama Platform FastTV With $32 Million Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round Palestinian filmmaker Shayma’ Awawdeh’s “The Story of the Mountain” and Syrian director Anas Zwahri’s “Their Ghosts Never Left My Home” received CFC’s two $10,000 jury awards for development and post-production, respectively. The Qatar Film Committee awarded four $25,000 grants to “Twelve Fig Leaves,” “Reda,” “Madness and Honey Days” and “Naydalaan.” Other projects secured a combination of cash grants, technical services and invitations to international markets, including Cannes’ Fantastic 7, Durban FilmMart and Medimed. Cairo Film Connection winners Courtesy of Cairo Film Festival Here is a closer look at some of the projects presented at this year’s Cairo Film Connection. Projects in Development “The Story of the Mountain” (Shayma’ Awawdeh, Palestine, France. Produced by Shayma’ Awawdeh) What would Palestinian children do if they could make the checkpoint separating their neighborhood from the rest of Hebron disappear? That question lies at the heart of “The Story of the Mountain,” a hybrid documentary in which children use filmmaking and fantasy to conceive of a reality different from their own. During a creative workshop, they imagine a magical mountain that transforms into a giant grandmother capable of destroying the checkpoint at the entrance to their neighborhood. Their fantasy becomes a way of envisioning a future free from the constraints of life under occupation. Awawdeh, whose short documentary “ Intersecting Memory ” opened IDFA in 2025 and won Clermont-Ferrand’s Grand Prix National in 2026, is seeking co-production partners and writing residencies. “Twelve Fig Leaves” (Joëlle Abou Chabké, Lebanon. Produced by Lara Abou Saïfan) In Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, filmmaker Joëlle Abou Chabké is exploring an ancestral method of weather prediction. Her documentary “Twelve Fig Leaves” follows her as she tests the Bawāhīr, a traditional Lebanese practice, while building a sustainable farm with her husband in his native village. The project explores the relationship between land, heritage and belonging amid political and environmental uncertainty. “This film lives at the intersection of climate collapse, war, ancestral knowledge and the deeply human need to belong somewhere,” Abou Chabké says. Produced by Lara Abou Saïfan’s Placeless Films (“ Dead Dog ”), the documentary received a $25,000 Qatar Film Committee grant, following AFAC development funding and a DocsBarcelona Pro Shared Shores Award at Beirut-based Aflamuna Connection. “Naydalaan” (Mariam Al-Dhubhani, Yemen, Jordan. Produced by Bassam Alasad) Drawing on her childhood experiences of sleep paralysis, Yemeni filmmaker Mariam Al-Dhubhani blends fantasy and psychological horror in “Naydalaan,” a feature set in 1990s Sana’a. The story follows 10-year-old Nadia into a nightmarish world where she encounters girls from different periods of Yemen’s history, confronting questions of identity, exclusion and belonging. “At a time when so much of Yemen is seen through destruction, I want to make room for its imagination, complexity and the many ways of belonging within it,” Al-Dhubhani says. The project received a $25,000 Qatar Film Committee grant and $10,000 in casting and sound-mixing services. Previously developed through the Doha Film Institute’s Feature Script Lab, it is seeking further financing and international co-producers. “The Schoolyard” (Mohamed Siam, Egypt, Belgium. Produced by Mohamed Siam and Brandy Miller) Five teenage boys navigate friendship, violence and shifting loyalties over the course of a turbulent school year in “The Schoolyard,” a fiction feature set in a crumbling public school on Cairo’s outskirts. “I learned early that the real lessons were often not in the classroom, but in power, fear, hierarchy and survival,” says director Mohamed Siam, who attended private, public and military schools in Egypt. Drawing on those experiences, he aims to capture “the humor, tenderness and imagination” that persist even in oppressive environments, exploring what happens when children are forced to grow up too soon. The project received a $10,000 cash award from ART, $30,000 in technical and development services and an invitation to Durban FilmMart. Shooting is planned for summer 2027. Siam’s previous films include “ Amal ,” which opened IDFA in 2017 and won the Golden Tanit at Carthage, and “My Father’s Scent,” which received multiple awards at Venice’s Final Cut program in 2024. “The Man Who Is Gone” (Naji Ismail, Egypt. Produced by Muhammad Taymour) Haunted by recurring nightmares and a deep sense of loss, a man in his 40s travels to Upper Egypt to fulfill his ailing mother’s wishes in “The Man Who Is Gone.” What begins as a family obligation takes a supernatural turn as he encounters a world of folklore and buried memories. Drawing on Upper Egypt’s traditions of myth and oral storytelling, writer and director Naji Ismail explores how grief shapes our relationship with the past, blurring the boundaries between the living and the dead. “At a time when we are often overwhelmed by the urgency of the present, returning to these inherited stories can remind us of the depth of our human experience and our place within a much longer history,” he tells Variety . The project received $9,000 in cash awards, additional development and post-production services and an invitation to Cannes’ Fantastic 7. Previously supported by the Doha Film Institute, it is targeting a late 2027 shoot. “Dwellers of the Cabins” (Hend Bakr, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar. Produced by Hend Bakr and Tamer Nady) Egyptian filmmaker Hend Bakr examines her Nubian heritage in “Dwellers of the Cabins,” a documentary about a community in Alexandria whose ancestors were displaced from southern Egypt in the early 20th century. Now threatened with demolition to make way for an investment project, the settlement where Bakr grew up has become the focus of her efforts to preserve her community’s history. “I am telling my own story and the struggle of my own family between preserving their culture and being included,” Bakr says. The documentary received $15,000 in sound and DCP mastering services and an invitation to Rough Cut Lab Africa. With approximately 30% of its financing secured, the project is targeting completion in 2028. “Terminus” (Oumaima Trabelsi, Tunisia. Produced by Oumaima Trabelsi and Erige Sehiri) Ten years after being deported from Italy, Sadok spends his days driving his taxi along the same 10-kilometer route through the Tunisian hometown he once hoped to escape. His repetitive journeys form the basis of “Terminus,” a documentary exploring the tension between returning home and the lingering desire to build a life elsewhere. “At a time when migration is often told through the act of leaving, I want to turn my gaze towards what comes after, and what remains of that longing once the journey is over,” director Oumaima Trabelsi says. The project received a $1,000 development award and $15,000 in sound and subtitling services. Previously supported by Tunisia’s Ministry of Culture, it is targeting completion in January 2028. “Dear Tarkovsky” (Firas Khoury, Sweden, Jordan, France. Produced by Linda Mutawi) Palestinian filmmaker Firas Khoury, whose debut feature “ Alam ” won three awards at CIFF in 2022, is developing “Dear Tarkovsky,” a tragicomedy about a filmmaker who stages a fake rescue to convince a wealthy man’s daughter to finance his debut about the acclaimed Soviet director, only to fall in love with her. “The film is a celebration of cinema,” Khoury says. “We, as Palestinians, have the right to put our name forward as explorers in art as well, not only as humanitarian cases.” Produced by Linda Mutawi’s Stockholm-based Fikra, the $3.5 million project previously received support from the Tunisian-Italian Fund, Malmö Industry Days and Durban FilmMart. It is seeking additional financing and co-production partners. “Their Ghosts Never Left My Home” Courtesy of Cairo Film Festival Projects in Post-Production “Their Ghosts Never Left My Home” (Anas Zwahri, France, Syria, Qatar, Lebanon. Produced by Ahmad Alhaj) For five Syrian mothers whose sons were forcibly disappeared under the Assad regime, the lack of closure has become part of everyday life. “Their Ghosts Never Left My Home” explores how the women preserve their sons’ memories while continuing to seek explanations about their fates. “Two years after the fall of the regime in Syria, the issue of the forcibly disappeared remains unaddressed,” Zwahri says. “Many families await answers from the new government, but their pleas go unanswered.” The documentary received CFC’s $10,000 post-production jury award and festival distribution services from Cult. Supported by AFAC, Aflamuna and the Doha Film Institute, it is targeting a 2027 premiere. “A Butterfly Hug” (Sally Abobasha, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Sweden. Produced by Aya Tallah Yusuf and Sally Abobasha) Filmed over six years in Cairo’s working-class neighborhoods, “A Butterfly Hug” follows Sajda, Shorouk, Shahd and Abdelrahman, young people living with epidermolysis bullosa, a rare genetic condition that makes their skin extremely fragile, as they navigate adolescence, friendship and family expectations. “What attracted me to them wasn’t their disease. It was their confidence, their laughter and their dreams,” director Sally Abobasha says. “They reminded me of myself as a teenager, although they were much braver than I was,” she adds. The documentary, filmed in a cinéma vérité style, secured $12,000 in cash grants from AH Media, Traveler and Stars Media, alongside $30,000 in post-production services and an invitation to Medimed, with completion targeted for early 2028. “Growing Up Twice” (Khaled Alkhaldi, Syria, Jordan. Produced by Lujain Hamdan. Co-produced by Deema Dabis) Set between Jordan’s Za’atari refugee camp and Amman, “Growing Up Twice” follows Baraa, a young Syrian mother who survived child marriage and is struggling to reclaim her independence while raising her son. As she attempts to build a new life, family pressures and “cycles of violence” force her to confront the difficult choices between personal freedom and motherhood. “This film became my act of rebellion, a way to turn my anger at the injustice and cruelty in this world into action,” producer Lujain Hamdan says. “As documentary filmmakers, we must learn how to approach these difficult stories and carry them to the world,” director Khaled Alkhaldi adds. The documentary received $6,000 in post-production services from Cult. title: How Iran’s Pegah Ahangarani Turned Her Family Archives Into a Regime-Challenging Oscar Hopeful
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 23, 2026 1:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Rehearsals for a Revolution' filmmaker Pegah Ahangarani Sony Pictures Classics “Cinema is not just part of my life,” begins Pegah Ahangarani. “It’s me, actually.” The director and actress grew up on film sets. Both of her parents were filmmakers themselves and immersed their children in the Iranian entertainment industry. Ahangarani became a child star, skyrocketing to fame at just 14 in 1999’s The Girl in the Sneakers . “I won a lot of awards,” she smiles to The Hollywood Reporter . But even she couldn’t have predicted the award-winning success of her debut feature-length documentary, Rehearsals for a Revolution . Related Stories Movies Record Number of International and Animated Features Oscar-Eligible This Season Music Don Toliver Postpones O2 Arena Show After Evacuation Due to "Unknown Substance" Released at Manchester Concert The Cannes-premiering — and L’Œil d’or-winning — project is a poignant reminder of the power of memory. Ahangarani, whose other essay documentaries include shorts I Am Trying to Remember (2021), My Father (2023) and Child Soldier (2024), sketches her entire life story in this latest work. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protest footage, newspapers and recorded voices, she retraces more than 40 years of Iran ’s turbulent history. From the late ’70s up until the war with the U.S. and Israel, Ahangarani pieces together and narrates intimate recollections from her life — the vanilla scent of her schoolteacher’s hair and desperate search for her uncle in videos from the 1999 Iranian student protests among them — that help to form the portrait of a country shaped by political repression, and in constant hope for a revolution. Personal is the operative word in this co-production between the Czech Republic and Spain. “I want to tell my audience: ‘Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility,'” says its director. As daunting as that task was — Ahangarani has already been arrested and spent time in the notorious Evin Prison, and expects not to be able to return to Iran at the risk of a lengthy jail sentence following the release of this film — she remains steadfast in her belief that using family archives is the greatest weapon at her disposal against the regime. “I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,'” says Ahangarani. “Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe.” Having left Iran in 2022, Ahangarani shares candid reflections with viewers about the guilt she’s experienced in the wake of this year’s civilian massacres and brutal crackdown on the Woman, Life, Freedom movement back home. From London, where she has been settled since 2023, Ahangarani talks to THR about putting that guilt up on screen — and being selected as the U.K.’s submission for best international feature film at the 2027 Oscars : “When you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land… [Now], there is one place that accepted me.” You grew up in film and TV. You were a child star. But when did you first realize you’d like to direct films yourself? I grew up in cinema, yes. All of the crew members were like my family members. I called them aunties and uncles. ( Laughs .) I cannot separate myself from cinema. Cinema is not just part of my life — it’s me, actually. I started cinema as my main career when I was 14. I acted in one film, The Girl in the Sneakers , and that film became very successful. I won a lot of awards. I was a teenager, and I was super happy. And then a few years after that, I remember I saw some documentaries and I thought, “OK, I’d like to maybe be a documentary filmmaker.” I made a few documentaries, but they were very naive. It [was] TV-style documentaries. Then I got familiar with [the] essay style in literature, and then I started exploring that style in some documentaries. I saw some Chris Marker documentaries for example, and Jonas Mekas. Pegah Ahangarani’s family photos feature heavily in ‘Rehearsals for a Revolution.’ Sony Pictures Classics You liked their style? I thought maybe I should find that style for myself, so six or seven years ago I made a short documentary with this style. I used personal archives and I used my voiceover as a narration, and I started making very personal documentaries. That film became very successful as well. The New Yorker published that documentary. It premiered at IDFA Film Festival and a lot of festivals after that. And then I made another short documentary, same style, and another one again. And then after those three documentaries, I started making this one. The archive of film and photos you use in this is just incredible. Is it daunting, or were you nervous, crafting an entire project around such intimate artefacts and stories? Yes, actually. ( Laughs .) I had a lot of concern about it, and not just for this film. […] A few years ago, when I was living in Iran, I went to my grandmother’s house, and I found some old family albums there. And I started looking through the photographs, and then I saw one photo. My mom was there. My father was there. I was there too. I was two or three years old, and I noticed a man who was standing next to my father, but his face had been scratched out. And I asked my grandmother, “Who is this person? Why has his face been scratched out?” She said, “He was your father’s best friend. He was executed after the revolution because he was a political prisoner.” And I realized my grandmother didn’t destroy the whole photo. She kept that photo, just scratched that face. After that shocking moment, I realized that maybe my responsibility as a documentary filmmaker is to find these old family photos, this personal footage, and find these scratched-out faces and bring them back to life, bring them back to the frame, and bring them back to our collective memory. After that, I thought a lot about these archives, and I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools.’ Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe. From that day, I started thinking about how I should use these materials as my facts. […] If you go deeper [into] one photograph, if you focus on it, you can see the part of our history in that photograph. But that wasn’t easy at all. When I made that short documentary, I sent it to my mother because my mother was one of the characters, my father was one of the characters, and I had a lot of concern because they might be in trouble after that film. But they were okay. I remember one thing: I sent my film to my grandmother, and I told her, “Okay, I made a short documentary based on the photo that you kept for me.” And she said, “Yes, maybe I kept that photo just for you to make this documentary.” This is a co-production between Spain and the Czech Republic, is that right? What work went into getting this over the line? Because using your own photos, films and narration, it strikes me as incredibly inexpensive documentary. [It was made] with nothing, actually. ( Laughs .) I had a producer [with whom] I made three of my short documentaries, Kaveh Farnam [founder of the Czech Republic’s Media Nest], and he’s an Iranian independent film [producer] outside of Iran. I remember when I was making a previous documentary, I found him, I texted him, and he joined the project. And that one was like this — I didn’t need money because I worked with my personal archives. But I wanted support for distribution [and] things. At that time, I was inside Iran, and I told Mr. Farnum that after this film, if I got arrested or something like that, please publish the film. I needed someone just for publishing. And then when I moved to London, I talked to Mr. Farnum about this feature film, and he said, “Okay, I’m in,” and I didn’t need any money for that. I just needed a small [amount of] money for my editor [Arash Ashtiani]. The Spain company [Fasten Films]… they found me and they wanted me to make another film for them. And then I told them, “I have one film, it’s finished now. I can send it to you, and if you want, you can join this project as well.” Right after they watched the film, they texted me and they told me, “Oh, we love the film. We want to join the project.” I see. They supported us because we needed some money for the copyright of the music and sound design, and they have a good relationship with a French distributor… Then they sent the film to the Cannes Film Festival, and they have a very good relationship with Cannes because they are French, and everything actually happened after that. But for the process of making this, we didn’t need any money. One standout part of the documentary, for me, is when you’re scrolling through some of those harrowing images and videos from this year’s protests and you talk about your guilt and trying to compensate for that with the film. What has it been like reckoning with that through these glamorous film festivals? Everything was very strange because right after the massacre, we were in the process of editing episode five. We wanted to show me [and] my new life as an immigrant, living in exile, and then war happened and massacre happened, and so we didn’t know how we should respond [to] these disasters in our film. That was a very complicated situation because I couldn’t focus on the film. I told my editor, “Cinema doesn’t mean [anything] anymore after all these dead bodies.” And then I realized that, “Okay, I should share all these concerns with my audience because this is the only way I should tell them.” But I didn’t have any idea that the the film [could] be successful. During the process of making this, it was just me and my editor, Arash, and a little mic, and a very intimate space. I remember the distribution company texted me and told me the director of Cannes, Thierry Frémaux, told us maybe you can be in the official selection. That was very exciting. That day, I just lay down on the sofa in our office… I couldn’t handle this much excitement. We realized we can compete with, for example, Steven Soderbergh, because he had a film in Cannes in the official documentary selection. And in Cannes, they told us, “You won the best documentary prize,” and I think I’m in the middle of some dream or something like that. Not because my film is successful now, but because I try to show these 40 years of Iranian history and this ongoing struggle of the Iranian people, and everybody around the world now can see this struggle. Rehearsals for a Revolution, directed by Pegah Ahangarani. Sony Pictures Classics What do you hope audiences are talking and thinking about after seeing this film? After the first screening in Cannes, I realized one thing, which was very sweet: When the film finished and people started clapping, many of them came and told me, “We think we love your people as much as you.” I thought, ‘So this is cinema.’ You can show something that people don’t have any idea about, and they can resonate with it, and they can feel this struggle. They can feel [for] your people, which is amazing. Many people, after watching the film, they think they know me very well [and that] they’re a friend of mine, which is very sweet. I think the film is successful because I could create a sense of intimacy. Through the narration and through the film, I want to tell my audience: “Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility.” This film is officially the U.K.’s official Oscar submission for best international feature. What does that mean to you? That was great news. Not just because of the film, but when you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land. When I left Iran, I thought, “OK, this is just a temporary situation.” And then I realized that no, maybe it’s permanent. I cannot go back anymore. I should accept my new life, and that was very difficult. When the U.K. announced that they picked our film … I had a feeling like I wasn’t stateless anymore. There is one place that accepted me. I’m sure you miss your family so much, but you don’t envision a future where you can return? When I left Iran in 2021, I didn’t have any plan to stay outside of Iran. I left my country with just one carry-on to participate in the IDFA Film Festival for my short documentary. And after the second screening, my mother, she was in Iran [and] called me and told me the regime had called her and asked her to interrogate me about the film. She told me, “Stay outside for a while, for one or two months.” And then the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement happened and I published a video to show my solidarity with that movement, and then my mother told me they sent a letter [saying] there is a court order against me. They seized my apartment and my bank accounts in Iran and I realized that I can’t go back. If I go back, I have to go to jail. I was in jail for one month in solitary [confinement], but if I go back, maybe I could be in jail for six or seven years or something like that. I decided to stay outside because I wanted to make my film. THR

title: Robert De Niro & Timothée Chalamet Will Close Out The Year As Hosts On ‘Saturday Night Live’

title: Macy Gray to Release Next Album Inside a Microdrama, Partnering With Vertical Platform ReelShort (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 23, 2026 1:00pm PT Macy Gray to Release Next Album Inside a Microdrama, Partnering With Vertical Platform ReelShort (EXCLUSIVE) By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest Meet Some of the Unsung Heroes Who Keep NBC Moving as It Celebrates 100 Years 3 days ago Taylor Swift’s ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Crime Scene Evidence Board from the Emmys Goes on Display at the Paley Center (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago As U.S. Infrastructure Crumbles, ABC’s ‘World News Tonight’ Posts Highest Week-Long Daily Ratings Since COVID 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Buckner/WWD In what vertical series platform ReelShort is billing as the first of its kind, recording artist Macy Gray plans to release her new album via an original scripted microdrama. The vertical series, titled “ The Trouble With the Truth ,” will star Gray and feature songs from her next album. ReelShort’s Sunflower Studio is behind “The Trouble With the Truth,” with casting currently underway for the series. The studio and platform plan to start production on the series in January 2027 and time the release to Gray’s album, which will also be titled “The Trouble With the Truth.” Gray is looking at a 2027 Q1 release for the new music. Related Stories India's T-Series and Hungama Launch Microdrama Platform FastTV With $32 Million Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round According to Sunflower Studio and ReelShort, the plan is to integrate Gray’s new songs into the series’ original dramatic narrative. Said the company in a release: “The partnership reflects ReelShort’s continued evolution as a destination for original storytelling while opening new possibilities for recording artists to introduce music, engage fans and expand their creative reach through scripted entertainment.” Added Sunflower Studio head Fiona Li: “Vertical drama has so much potential beyond traditional storytelling, and this partnership is an exciting step toward exploring what’s possible. Collaborating with an iconic artist like Macy Gray allows us to push the boundaries of the format, bringing vertical drama into the world of music and opening up new ways for artists and audiences to connect.” Gray first hit the scene in 1999 with her first album, “On How Life Is,” which was certified three-time platinum by the RIAA, earning her a Grammy for best female pop vocal performance for the song “I Try.” Other hits from the release included “Why Didn’t You Call Me,” “Do Something” and “Still.” Gray has released 10 studio albums and one live album. “The Trouble With the Truth” reps Gray’s first new album release in nearly a decade; her last album, “Ruby,” was put out in 2018. title: ‘SNL’ Sets Timothée Chalamet and Robert De Niro as Final Hosts of 2026

De Niro will headline “SNL” for the fourth time on Dec. 12 with musical guest Slayyyter, who makes her debut at Studio 8H. title: ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ Stars Christopher Briney & Michelle Randolph Talk Comedy’s “Important” Presence In Script And How They Built Their Characters
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Steven Spielberg To Helm ‘Heart In Winter’ With Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy & Mark Rylance; Paul Thomas Anderson Scripting For Focus Read the full story By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi All The Songs In ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ From Sabrina Carpenter To Olivia Rodrigo Everything We Know About Amazon MGM & Sony Pictures TV’s ‘God Of War’ Adaptation So Far ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Denée Benton Talks Peggy’s “Victory Lap” & “Ambitious Tension” In Her Marriage To Dr. Kirkland View All November 23, 2026 1:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Michell Randolph and Christopher Briney in 'Clashing Through The Snow' Prime Video In Prime Video’s latest original Christmas romantic comedy, Clashing Through the Snow , Christopher Briney ( The Summer I Turned Pretty) and Michell Randolph ( Landman ) portray rival editors whose relationship takes an enemies to lovers arc during a road trip to New York . Ryan Mitchell (Briney) and Hannah Hendricks both hear from their boss Jeremy (P.J. Byrne) separately that layoffs loom at Latitude Publishing, where they will compete for a merged version of their roles in the new year. The ambitious employees then both set up secret meetings with prospective authors that could respectively land them the job, but require travel to New York city over the Christmas holiday. The pair exhibit fundamentally different taste in books and what they aim to sell, but their shared love of reading provides them common ground on which to bond when a winter storm forces them together during their grounded travels to the east coast. Related Stories News All The Songs In ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ From Sabrina Carpenter To Olivia Rodrigo Books 7 New Christmas Movies Coming Out In 2026 From ‘Ebenezer’ To ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ “Ryan’s sort of an interesting case because he’s obviously like, ‘How do we market this and how do we make this sellable and profitable?’ But he loves books. There’s a big part of his heart — and they get into it in the movie — that appreciates literature, and really he just wants people to read books,” Briney said of his character, who leans more into numbers and trends. “That’s what it’s about. It’s not really about money. It’s about exposure. At least that was sort of my approach to it. It’s about, ‘How can we get more people to read books?’ which I admire and appreciate in him.” Watch on Deadline A good visual representation of Ryan lies in a snapshot of his home, where he has framed photos with Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins and Divergent author Veronica Roth. He also mentions his discovering Fourth Wing author Rebecca Yarros two years after it happened. Michelle’s editor Hannah tends to go for the more niche, Awards-bait books that are high brow. “She’s a literary traditionalist. I remember when I first booked [the role], I was like, ‘I’ve got to read Virginia Woolf,’ because she talks about how that’s who raised her. I love that Hannah’s whole thing is, ‘I just want whatever people are reading to mean something,’ for there to be a real purpose behind it,” Randolph told Deadline. “And I’ve I’ve definitely thought about what books would Hannah love and what authors, like Jane Austen. I think that she would read a lot of the classics. Joan Didion. And it definitely made me want to read more classics.” In the below interview, the stars also break down their reactions to the script, Briney’s Jim Carrey-like approach to physical comedy, Hannah’s career focus, working with Lukas Gage, Buc-ees knockoff Luc-ees and more: DEADLINE: Had you both read this script before signing on to the project? What drew you to doing an original Christmas rom com, and especially this one, when rom coms are starting to get rebooted nowadays? MICHELLE RANDOLPH : I read the script multiple times before I signed on to the project. I actually I have this app called Speechify, and I remember I got the script and I was driving and I was like, ‘I just really want to read it right now. ‘So I listened to it for the first time with Gwyneth Paltrow reading it/speaking it to me. And then once once I got home, I sat down and I actually went through it, a very different experience, but it’s such a joyful, fun script. It’s silly. It’s absurd. I love [that] both the characters have a real emotional core and very specific personalities. I love this script. CHRISTOPHER BRINEY: It made me laugh, and I think it’s really sweet, but I loved that that comedy was an important character in in this script, and it felt like a fun, challenging project, and it was certainly challenging and certainly fun. L-R: Christopher Briney and Michelle Randolph in ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ Prime Video DEADLINE: Chris, I feel like you really leaned into the physical comedy of this one. BRINEY: I hope it’s funny, dude. I might like look like an idiot. DEADLINE: No, that’s not what I’m saying! Could you talk more about the challenge of that and how it was fun to explore that as an actor? BRINEY: Yeah, I mean, it was really fun. I think that the first couple weeks on a project, you’re always finding your footing, and there was some like physicality to Ryan that that I think somewhere in there I had found, and there were some things that Carlson said about… RANDOLPH: Jim Carrey. BRINEY: Right, there were some Jim Carrey moments, and there was like this scene that we shot at Webster Hall when I’m handing the paper through the [glass barricade], and there was just something about how cool he thinks he is, and how like flimsy he really is that really unlocked a lot of that character for me. It was fun. It was really fun. I loved it. DEADLINE: Michelle, I wanted to ask you too how you know Hannah’s very career focused versus l love life, and I feel like that’s just really relatable for a lot of women right now. I’m curious your thoughts and what you wanted to bring out in her to make her more more than just that ? RANDOLPH: Yeah, I love how ambitious she is and passionate. Books are her life. Her authors — she’s so invested in her career. She’s a literary purist, and I think that passion in someone is so admirable. I also think that’s what makes it really sweet when you can see the moments in the movie when she starts to fall for Ryan because it’s the first time she’s letting herself not take her work so seriously. It’s a protection, throwing yourself into work, it’s like, “Oh well, I’m distracted and I don’t have time for it, so that’s why I’m not with somebody.” I think slowly she realizes, “I can have both.” There’s a balance. DEADLINE: What was it like filming at Luc-ee’s, which I don’t know if you’ve been to a Buc-ee’s, but how did it compare if you have? RANDOLPH: Oh my gosh. BRINEY: I’ve never been to a Buc-ee’s. RANDOLPH: I went for the first time. BRINEY: Is it good? I mean, I’m familiar with the idea and how awesome it appears to be. RANDOLPH: It’s magical. There are so many Bucky’s because I film in Texas most of the year, and there’s a bunch. I always pass them on the way to set, and I went for the first time with my cast, and we all got the pajamas, the onesie. We all got Bucky’s onesies and all the snacks and it’s huge. It’s like Costco where they have gas, they have car washes… BRINEY: I’m more familiar with like Cumberland Farms and Wawa on roadtrips. I feel like Wawa’s maybe junior Buc-ee’s. Wawa’s great. I support Wawa. L-R: Christopher Briney, Michelle Randolph and Lukas Gage in ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ Prime Video DEADLINE: What was it like working with Lukas Gage in that smaller role? BRINEY: He was insane. RANDOLPH: We’ve never broken more. BRINEY: I could not keep it together. I really couldn’t. I am sure that there’s evidence of that. RANDOLPH: It’s in the movie, which it’s like Hannah and Ryan are laughing at the absurdity of what Lukas Gage’s character is. But I also know that it was actually Chris and Michelle in that coverage, we broke. BRINEY: He’s so funny, man. title: Inside the ‘Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic’: A Recipe for Blending Brands With TV (and a Full-Circle Career Moment for Host Drew Barrymore)
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All November 23, 2026 12:52pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Drew Barrymore, left, talks with baker Legenia Bearden in CBS' 'Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic.' Heidi Gutman/CBS The folks behind CBS ‘ Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic are hoping to make this holiday special an annual Thanksgiving week tradition. “I feel like this is going to become part of our cultural tradition,” says Scott Weintrob, founder of Studio Large Eyes and executive producer of the special. “Every Thanksgiving for the next 10 years, with the Pillsbury Bake-Off as the trigger to Thanksgiving week.” The show is actually a collaboration between CBS and General Mills — which, incidentally, owns the “Bake-Off” trademark in the United States. (“Which is why they cannot call The Great British Bake Off the Bake Off in the U.S. and they have to call it The Great British Baking Show, ” says Lisa Balzo, head of brand studio partnerships at General Mills .) Related Stories TV 'Survivor 51' Star Lewis Kelly on His $1 Million Coin Flip and Joining the Cast at the Last Minute TV CBS Inks New Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors In developing the special, Weintrob drew on his background in advertising, which has included award-winning work with Rihanna (he designed and directed Amazon’s Emmy-winning Savage x Fenty show) along with Lewis Hamilton x Ferris Bueller’s Day Off, reimagining the film’s classic valet scene with Lewis Hamilton, Edward Norton and Ferrari, which went viral. (He also recently directed and produced Mr. T: I Pity the Fool for Netflix and created Orlando Bloom: To the Edge for Peacock.) Weintrob’s company, Studio Large Eyes, aims to create brand-inspired entertainment with the philosophy “entertainment first, marketing second.” He says his background crossing both advertising and TV gives him a unique perspective to understand both parties and what their objectives are. “They are quite different,” he says. “And they have different approaches. Being able to talk to networks and streamers and also being able to talk to global brands. I had this in-between knowledge because they are different in so many ways but they all are trying to do the same thing, so I was perfectly positioned to be the conduit.” Drew Barrymore hosts CBS’ Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic. Virginia Sherwood/CBS Balzo notes that GM, parent company of Pillsbury, had been interested in the idea of a “big grand spectacle” that would incorporate one of the company’s brands. She had already met Weintrob previously at an industry event, and the two began having conversations about some options. “I started talking [with Weintrob] about the history of the Bake-Off, and how it used to be this kind of big grand spectacle that was put on as a live event,” she says. “Over the years, we’ve done various different things with it, and it’s become a smaller digital activation. We’ve also collaborated with the Food Network. I mentioned to Scott that we have been talking about, for years, wanting to bring it back to its full glory. And he pitched this incredible live event.” “What I originally said to them was, I love the format of the Westminster Dog Show as a baking show, a large event as a live, two-hour special focusing on ordinary people doing extraordinary things,” Weintrob recalls. They agreed on the idea and decided that Thanksgiving would be a key time for the project to air. “I felt we had the opportunity to go and talk to distributors about making this wonderful event. And that’s the key word: It’s an event.” Balzo says the concept “felt so perfect” and “felt very serendipitous to me at the time. He had this project in his head that that was so perfectly aligned with Pillsbury and what we were looking to do with the Bake Off.” Back to that trademark: Pillsbury held its first Bake-Off in 1949, when it was called Pillsbury’s Best Grand National Baking Contest. A total of 100 finalists went to New York to compete, and each received at least $100 and kept the G.E. stove they baked on. Eleanor Roosevelt presented the grand prizes, which ranged from $25,000 to $50,000. In the 1970s and ’80s, the show hit TV and then began expanding to other cities, from Honolulu to Houston. Bob Barker hosted the broadcasts on CBS, with prizes set at $40,000 in the 1980s. Winning recipes were published in print advertisements for folks at home. (Fun fact: Peanut Blossoms, those peanut butter-flavored cookies with a Hershey’s kiss in the middle, were first introduced by finalist Freda Smith in 1957, and it is one of nine recipes in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.) In the ’90s, Kurt Wait became the first $1 million grand prize, and the first male to win the title. Phylicia Rashad became the Bake-Off ’s first female host in 2000, and then the Bake-Off moved into the digital era along with a stint on Food Network. Baker Sam McCabe in CBS’ Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic. Virginia Sherwood/CBS Balzo says that baking competitions are immensely watchable because it offers inspiration for viewers at home. “The recipes they’re making are so relatable, and I think people are really going to feel that when they’re watching” the new show, she said, adding that many brands are trying to get into this space, and for GM, the Bake-Off special offers an “authentic connection” with Pillsbury. “It feels like bringing back something that people have already experienced and want more of, as opposed to trying to advertise through content like this.” For 2026’s Bake-Off, Weintrob began assembling a production team and then setting up meetings with distributors. “When network TV is involved, the word ‘spectacle’ is a brilliant word as a reference point,” he shares. “It needs to be a spectacle to work on network, and CBS saw just how great the show could be. They were the perfect partner to work with.” With CBS on board, they set about finding a host. Having read General Mills’ Wikipedia page “to the end,” Weintrob learned that Drew Barrymore had appeared in a Pillsbury commercial (for its pre-made chocolate-chip cookie dough) at age 4. “I called up Pillsbury and said, ‘Drew has an incredible daytime show. Drew’s gotta be the host,'” Weintrob shares. “[For] the build to a show, it can’t just be about the show. You’ve gotta get people to watch, there is amplification, there is social. This is all the responsibility of myself and my studio. With Drew, the idea was, play the commercial on your [talk] show, and announce it to the world.” Balzo agrees. She cites Barrymore’s authenticity and relatability as two qualities that make her a great host. “Drew authentically remembers that experience [of the commercial], and the brand means something to her,” Balzo says. “She really cares about that connection and the authenticity to the brand in this partnership, and I think people will see that come through on screen when they watch the special, which is why we’re so excited to have her as our host. [In addition], we wanted this to be about more than just baking. We want to tell the stories of a diverse set of people and their backstories and what baking means to them and memories mean to them. And she’s the perfect host to pull those stories out of our contestants. It was incredible to watch her on set because it felt like she was having just this intimate conversation with [the bakers]. I think they felt that too.” Twenty-four home bakers will compete on Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic, scheduled to air on the CBS Television Network. Drew Barrymore is pictured, center. Heidi Gutman/CBS Weintrob and showrunner Brielle Cohen watched 250 submissions from home bakers to cull the list down to 24 competitors who all have “incredible” backstories to share. In addition, famed baker and author Amirah Kassem will join Barrymore and celebrity chef judges Christina Tosi and Dook Chase in the special. It was filmed live on Oct. 23, he shares, which meant a tight turnaround for the Nov. 23 airdate. For her part, Balzo says this was the first time General Mills had done anything “on this scale,” so they really leaned on Weintrob and the production team to guide them through the process, though GM did play a hand in everything from creative direction to final casting to set direction to the judges and host. Execs also saw all the cuts and provided feedback. ( Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic is produced by Studio Large Eyes, Pantheon Media Group and Juma Entertainment. Executive producers include Weintrob for Studio Large Eyes, Jennifer O’Connell, Ariel Brozell, Eden Sutley and Martha Chaput for Pantheon, Robert Horowitz for Juma Entertainment and Brielle Cohen is showrunner. Balzo, Kenzie Caron and Eleanor Harkness serve as executive producers for Pillsbury.) Weintrob says having a strong relationship with brands is going to be important in the future of TV and advertising. “We are not reinventing the wheel,” he acknowledges. “Brands and television have always been connected. Pairing a brand with entertainment is the job of someone like myself. I see incredible opportunity because brands have very clear audiences that they want to get towards. This is what I call brand-inspired entertainment, which is there for the new consumer. It satisfies the existing consumer, but it also offers tremendous opportunity to reach a consumer that may not have heard of General Mills, Pillsbury, their cookies, their variety of product. Especially through this family-friendly show, it’s perfect for that brand.” A baked created from CBS’ Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic . Virginia Sherwood/CBS But, he adds, it’s not just matching a brand with a network and assuming the magic will happen. He says there is a lot of listening on his end and working with the brand to understand what they need while at the same time creating something that’s right for a distributor and their audience. “You’ve got to create bespoke entertainment for a brand,” he summarizes. “You can’t just send them random ideas.” There’s also the challenge of the promotional timeline for brands vs. distributors. Brands usually begin working on their promotional campaigns months out, while the distributors work on a shorter timeline, sometimes even just weeks. Weintrob says he worked with both companies to come up with an approach that benefited each of them. Both Weintrob and Balzo hope this special becomes an annual tradition that families can enjoy for years. And, Weintrob suggests, the special could expand to include Valentine’s Day or Super Bowl editions, for example. “As a brand and especially the Pillsbury brand, the whole family is so important,” Balzo adds. “So we wanted to make sure that we created something that could be one of those moments to bring families together around and create memories around.” Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic airs Nov. 23 from 8-10 p.m. ET/PT on CBS and streams on Paramount+ (Premium). title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Lands Season 5 Renewal at Apple TV
full_text: Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All November 23, 2026 12:31pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brendan Hunt, Tanya Reynolds and Jason Sudeikis in 'Ted Lasso' season four. Apple TV Logo text Ted Lasso , the series, is returning — even if Ted Lasso, the character, might be stepping away (slightly) from the soccer pitch. Apple TV has picked up a fifth season of the Emmy-winning comedy, which remains one of the streamer’s biggest shows. Season four, which concluded in early October, is on track to be one of the most viewed original streaming series of 2026; it spent 12 weeks on Nielsen’s top 10 streaming charts, drawing about 9.8 billion minutes of viewing time in that span. Not yet nailed down is who among the show’s large ensemble will be returning for season five: Final determinations about which castmembers will continue have yet to be made. A writers room for season five opened recently. Related Stories TV 'Presumed Innocent' Season 2 Pairs Rachel Brosnahan With Matthew Rhys in First Look at Next Courtroom Face-Off Business Apple TV Bulks Up With Video Podcasts The season four finale of Ted Lasso set up a number of avenues for the show to explore. After being lured back to London to coach AFC Richmond’s women’s team, Ted ( Jason Sudeikis ) stepped back from the job in the final episode, demoting himself to assistant manager so that Alice (Tanya Reynolds) could take the head job. Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham) also successfully fended off a challenge to her ownership of the club, and Roy (Brett Goldstein) took the reins at Chelsea while waiting to become a parent with Keeley (Juno Temple). The season four cast also features Brendan Hunt, Jeremy Swift, Jude Mack, Faye Marsay, Rex Hayes, Aisling Sharkey, Abbie Hern and Grant Feely Warner Bros. TV and Universal TV produce Ted Lasso . Sudeikis and Hunt executive produced season four with Joe Kelly, Jane Becker, Jamie Lee, Bill Wrubel, Jack Burditt, Goldstein, Leann Bowen, Bill Lawrence, Jeff Ingold and Liza Katzer. Sarah Walker and Phoebe Walsh served as writers and producers for season four, with Sasha Garron as co-producer. The writers room also included Julia Lindon and story editor Dylan Marron. Sudeikis, Lawrence, Kelly and Hunt developed the series, based on characters created for NBC Sports. THR

title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Renewed For Season 5 By Apple TV

Its targeted production start date is April 14, I hear. The renewal, which has been pending since the Season 4 finale was released in early October, was never in doubt — four seasons in, Ted Lasso remains Apple TV’s biggest global hit. Related Stories News All The Songs In ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 News ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Finale Recap: The Last Match Of The Season & A Shareholders’ Showdown But because Ted Lasso has been such a big juggernaut, comes from an outside studio, Warner Bros. Television, and has an executive producer and star, Jason Sudeikis , who is very protective of his creation, deals on the show have never been quick and easy, especially when it comes to Sudeikis’ contract. Further complicating the process this time was the fact that the Season 4 finale dropped the same day as Warner Bros. TV parent Warner Bros. Discovery’s acquisition by Paramount closed, so the renewal conversation was going on with the post-merger integration in the background. Sudeikis signing on for Season 4 paved the way to the renewal, with a writers room now starting up. As Deadline reported , the Ted Lasso team opted not to open a writers room ahead of the Season 4 renewal so the stories for next season have not been fleshed out. Watch on Deadline Because of that, character story arcs are yet to be locked in but it’s safe to assume that stars/co-creators Sudeikis (Ted Lasso) and Brendan Hunt (Coach Beard) would be back, joined by fellow OGs Hannah Waddingham (Rebecca), Jeremy Swift (Higgins), Brett Goldstein (Roy) and Juno Temple (Keeley) as well as at least some of the new Season 4 additions, most notably breakout Tanya Reynolds as Coach Alice Chilton. The renewal comes with a question about the extent of the involvement of Goldstein, who has two other series, Apple TV’s Shrinking , on which he is co-creator, executive producer and recurring guest star, and Prime Video’s upcoming Escorted, which he created, executive produces and headlines, in addition to his movie career. The uncertainty extends to how much we will see of Temple, who plays Roy’s girlfriend — and Rebecca’s BFF.

Apple TV announced Monday that it has given a Season 5 pickup to the hit Jason Sudeikis comedy from Warner Bros. TV. News wasn’t a surprise, given how well the Season 4 revival did for Apple TV; it just came down to striking a new deal with Sudeikis and Warner Bros. to continue the show. Sudeikis is back as star and executive producer. On a recent episode of the podcast “Talk Easy With Sam Fragoso,” Sudeikis expressed an interest in continuing “Ted Lasso” through Seasons 5 and 6, making for another three-season arc. title: John Turturro Says ‘Transformers’ Paychecks Helped Fund His Passion Projects, But Too Many Blockbusters Can Make You ‘Lose Your Inner Life’
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 23, 2026 12:28pm PT John Turturro Says ‘Transformers’ Paychecks Helped Fund His Passion Projects, But Too Many Blockbusters Can Make You ‘Lose Your Inner Life’ By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest Rian Johnson, a Vocal AI Critic, Warns Against Totally ‘Demonizing’ AI and Says His ‘Poker Face’ Revival With Peter Dinklage Is Dead 7 hours ago Jeff Goldblum, Marion Cotillard and John Turturro Dine With Morocco’s HRH Prince Moulay Rachid at Starry Royal Gala During Marrakech Film Festival 1 day ago Rian Johnson Cites Curry Barker as Reason to Be Optimistic About Future of Indie Filmmaking: ‘Youtube Is Just What Sundance Was in the ’80s’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection John Turturro may have earned some of his biggest paychecks from Michael Bay’s “Transformers” franchise, but the actor says there’s a danger in doing too many Hollywood blockbusters. Speaking at the Marrakech International Film Festival about his decision to join the blockbuster franchise, Turturro recalled advice he received from Robert Redford, who directed him in the 1994 film “Quiz Show.” Related Stories India's T-Series and Hungama Launch Microdrama Platform FastTV With $32 Million Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round “He said, ‘It’s good to work both sides of the street,'” Turturro said, referring to lucrative studio projects versus more personal, creative pursuits. “You can cross the street, and you can always go back as long as you don’t do too much of it in a row.” Turturro explained that spending too much time on commercial projects can come at the expense of an actor’s creative instincts. “What happens is you can lose your inner life,” he said. “You want to feed your inner life. That’s like your fireplace. You want to feed that.” The actor, who played the eccentric Agent Seymour Simmons in four “Transformers” films between 2007 and 2017, said the franchise required a different creative approach than his independent work. “It’s not like a fine painting. It’s more like when Picasso does the quick sketch type of thing, and you’ve got to kind of do it like you’re playing with your kids,” Turturro said. “There’s a challenge to that. Can you do that or not?” He added that “Michael Bay liked working with me because I basically play a version of him in some ways.” The actor also acknowledged — not for the first time — the financial benefits of taking on a major Hollywood franchise. “They pay me a lot more money, so then I can do all these other projects,” he said. Turturro recalled how his children encouraged him to take the “Transformers” role after years of turning down big-budget studio offers. In one instance, he passed on a substantial paycheck for the 1999 superhero comedy “Mystery Men” after his daughter read the script and gave him a less-than-enthusiastic review. “They offered me a ton of money. I’ve never made this much money,” Turturro said but when he showed his daughter the script she called it “garbage.” At the time, Turturro was also considering a stage production of Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot.” After reading the first eight pages of the play together, his daughter had a very different reaction: “This is good. This is very good.” Turturro ultimately chose the play, where he earned just $300 a week. Turtorro concluded with a final analogy: “I consider myself a plumber in my real work, and [commercial movies] are sort of my electrical job.” Turturro’s latest project, “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” also screened at Marrakech following his Golden Star tribute on Sunday night . Directed by Noah Segan and produced by Rian Johnson and Ram Bergman’s T-Street, the indie crime drama stars Turturro as an aging pickpocket struggling to make ends meet in a rapidly changing New York City. The film, which also stars Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito and Tatiana Maslany, premiered at Sundance earlier this year and was acquired by Sony Pictures Classics. title: ‘East of Eden’ Star Hoon Lee on the “Honor” of Playing Lee and Why It Made Sense to Expand on the Character
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All November 23, 2026 12:23pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hoon Lee stars as Lee in Netflix's adaptation of 'East of Eden.' Shane McCauley “It’s a huge relief,” says Hoon Lee of the reaction to East of Eden . “With any production, people work very hard. But I think this one in particular, there was the weight of expectation and wanting to honor the source material that adds a slightly different dimension.” The actor stars as Lee in Zoe Kazan’s adaptation of the classic John Steinbeck novel, released last month. The Florence Pugh-fronted series was quickly met with praise. “It almost would’ve been worse if it came out with a sort of indifference, like met with a wave of shrugging,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter . “To be well received the way the project has is obviously the best possible outcome and it’s very, very gratifying.” Related Stories Critics' Conversation The Best Fall TV Shows Hurt So Good TV Florence Pugh Was "So Nervous" to Release 'East of Eden' and Still Hasn't Read the Reviews: "It Was Too Much With This One" The series is very much aligned with the novel, but one of the most significant changes came in the form of the expansion of Lee’s character. He’d been given a head’s up, but he wasn’t sure just how in-depth the story would go until he received the scripts. All he knew was that Kazan and writer Alexander Chee had written a standalone episode for the character, the footage for which ended up being woven into other episodes. The actor was delighted to see what Kazan had to add and challenges anyone that questions just what the writer knows about the material. “That’s a huge risk for Zoe and the production but that actually speaks a lot to the boldness of her interpretation. There’s a lot of courage there, not only to put that forth, but to do it for the right reasons,” he says. “I don’t think anyone in the world knows this text better than Zoe. Every move she’s made, there is a reason for it, and there’s a justification in the text,” he continues. “She’s not somebody that is wildly going off script and going off the range to do what she’s doing. It’s a 600- to 800-page book. The idea that any of us who have just read it have all of the detail at our fingertips … But Zoe kind of does. She’s gone to that level.” Lee on the show’s positive reaction: “It’s very, very gratifying.” Shane McCauley The series, much like the novel, is quite heavy. It’s clear from moment one that show isn’t holding any punches. It might not be the easiest to watch in one go. “There should be a dosage that’s recommended,” he says somewhat cheekily. “It is intense.” Below, the actor speaks with THR about expanding upon the character of Lee, Kazan’s understanding of the material and how much he loves the character. What did you think about the decision to add more to Lee as a character? [Zoe’s] interpretation is deeply founded in the text, and it is expanded upon. But that choice, to me, speaks to the central ideas of the book itself, the sort of deep wells of humanism that Steinbeck brings. This idea that if we are going to use this book and talk about the thematics of this book — about what it means to be human and to have agency and to have choice — then it’s a totally viable thing to me. To make more human the people that at that time would’ve been somewhat marginalized or reduced — women, people of color. It’s certainly bold, but I think it’s in keeping with what she wanted to do for the entire production. It seems like you’ve gained a real respect for this material. Was there any anxiety about bringing this to life? There’s always the normal anxiety, which just revolves around variables and questions that you just don’t have visibility to at the time. We all could have shown up in New Zealand and hated each other, or we could have realized that we had six dollars to make seven episodes. Those sorts of things. But the added responsibility of the text, that’s a challenge I want. I want to have to do a good job because it’s important to you and because it’s important to other people. Where I knew we would encounter some friction is the more that people love any artwork, anything that’s important to them, whether that’s novels or movies or people or friendships, the more they protect it and the more they want their self-actualized canonical version to remain. There’s certainly a pressure there, but that’s just not how I view this situation. I can’t convince people to view it my way if they’re not inclined to. But I just feel that on its face, the idea of even attempting to create a one-to-one analog from novel to film or novel to television series is just flatly impossible. That’s true for any story. For any story. They’re just so wildly different in how they work, and how we participate with those mediums. We create the world in a novel. We not only create every detail of the world based on our own assumptions or preferences, we also create a hierarchy of importance. We create the hierarchy of attention to things. If you resonate with a character, that character looms larger in the story even with nothing changed in the words on the page. A film or a television show are exactly the opposite. It’s one collective production’s view on what is important and what you have to pay attention to, down to controlling what your eye focuses on. When you think about that level of control, there’s no way these things can match up. It’s not a task worth pursuing, which is part of the reason why I never watched the ’50s movie with James Dean. I knew that Lee was not included in that iteration. The actor on playing Lee: “It’s an honor. I love this character.” Shane McCauley What do you think about that? Certainly, that’s an omission. I have skin in that game literally. But I also think, well, what an interesting time capsule because in making that choice, Elia Kazan is saying, this is what I think is essential in the story. We have that reading, we have that perspective. In contrast, Zoe is doing the same thing. She’s saying, “This is what I think is important in this story and how I feel it, and when I read it, what I took from it.” That’s what we’re supposed to do. There’s an illusion that’s created, particularly in modern film and TV, that the details of the production, including the people who make it, are larger than the story or larger than the characters. In a book like this, that’s not the case. It’s much more like theater in that way. But you and I, we could do our own versions of Hamlet. We would be participants in a long lineage of people that have done Hamlet, and the role lives above us. We step into that river and step out. In film and TV, it feels to people like a character and an actor are fused, and that prevents people from reexamining it that easily. We should reexamine it. We should reinterpret, especially important stories and deeply felt stories. We should periodically reinterpret them because that’s their value to us, is to re-lens the same issues that we wrestle with in a new context, in our context, in our modern context, and remind us of things that we already feel deeply. What a wonderful lens to at it. Lee is a character that’s an essential to the story, in my reading of it. It seems Zoe agrees and you do as well. Well, it’s nice to have peaked now. There’s a lot of clarity. Better now than when I was 28, and it’s a long slide down the hill. It’s an honor. I love this character. I think the character is just a phenomenally realized human being at a time when I did not anticipate that, which perhaps speaks more to my own lack of awareness and shortsightedness, honestly. It’s also a good reminder that we broadly generalize, we coarse grain so many things and that in the detail there’s openings to a better understanding of the actual complexity that we’re wrestling with all the time and have wrestled with throughout our history. It’s easy for me as a person of color to … it’s an easy trap to paint with a very broad brush about opportunities I feel like haven’t been given, things like that. I was just talking about this, but when Lee says there’s a beauty in the truth, even if it’s a dreadful beauty — we are in a time and a place where we have a very difficult relationship with the idea of truth, partially because some people have been betrayed by that and partially because some people think truth is weaponized against them in some way and partially because the truth in and of itself is often difficult to confront. Without creating a foundation based upon the truth, how do we build anything with any integrity? How do we move forward? To bring it down to the most trivial levels, if I look at my own work somewhere and I just pat myself on the back for it, it’ll be very difficult for me to get better. There’s something very, very beautiful about this idea that in looking at this story and in looking at how Steinbeck was able to humanize his character, it prevents me from having the easy out of saying, “Well, everyone at a certain time period felt a certain way and everyone was… There were just amazing people with incredibly broad understandings of humanity at every point.” That’s something to remind ourselves that. If you’re someone that feels like you’re marginalized and struggling, you had allies at every point and maybe they weren’t given voice and maybe there weren’t many of them, but it doesn’t help us to feel like the monolith is out there and could come back at any time. I just don’t think that that’s fair, and I don’t think it’s accurate. THR

title: FCC To Vote On Plan To Relax Local TV And Radio Ownership Limits
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Steven Spielberg To Helm ‘Heart In Winter’ With Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy & Mark Rylance; Paul Thomas Anderson Scripting For Focus Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted FCC To Vote On Plan To Relax Local TV And Radio Ownership Limits Democratic National Committee Plans 12 Presidential Primary Debates Starting In June CBS News Staffers Take Buyout Offers As Skydance Looks For Cost Savings View All November 23, 2026 12:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brendan Carr Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The FCC plans to vote next month on a proposal to further relax ownership limits on broadcasters, this time targeting a rule that limits the number of stations a company can own in one market. The proposal would allow for TV and radio broadcasters to exceed those limits on a case-by-case basis and if the agency determines that it will “promote the public interest,” with criteria including diversity and localism. Currently, a company can own up to two stations in the same market. If the proposal is adopted, companies would no longer have to abide by the “subcaps” that restrict the balance of FM and AM stations they own in a market. Related Stories News Donald Trump Puts Himself At Center Of Jensen Huang's Reinstatement, Downplays "Sex Sells" Scandal Amid National Security Concerns News Democratic National Committee Plans 12 Presidential Primary Debates Starting In June The proposal is the latest effort to modify ownership rules under chairman Brendan Carr , who has said that he wanted to increase the leverage of local stations compared to national networks. The FCC proposal would keep in place a rule that prohibits any one entity from owning two broadcast networks. Watch on Deadline Last summer, the FCC voted to abandon a rule that limits a company from collectively owning stations covering more than 39% of the country. Carr wrote in a blog post that the change is needed because the “media marketplace has changed dramatically in recent years, yet many FCC regulations remain stuck in the past.” He wrote, “This item completes a long overdue effort to modernize those local broadcast ownership rules so that local TV and radio stations can continue to compete into the future. This will empower local broadcasters to grow stronger, invest in their communities, and deliver the news and information Americans rely on every day.” An FCC official denied that the vote on the proposal had to do with the change in control in Congress, with Democrats holding substantial majorities starting in January. When the FCC approved Nexstar’s merger with Tegna last March, it granted a waiver to allow the combined company to control more than two stations in a number of markets. That merger, though, is being challenged in court on antitrust grounds, and a judge had granted an injunction that requires that the companies be kept separate. More to come.
