title: ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians’: How Season 3 Brings Epic Moments to Life and Deals With Annabeth’s Absence in the Books
full_text: Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content From left: Percy Jackson and the Olympians- The Titan’s Curse’ and a still from Disney’s ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians’ show. Disney Hyperion;Disney/David Bukach Logo text Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’ s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it. *** Percy Jackson is back. Season 3 of the Disney+ /Hulu series Percy Jackson and the Olympians continues the saga of the Greek gods, their demigod offspring and the mission to prevent the rise of the Titans. The storyline is based on The Titan’s Curse , the third book in Rick Riordan ‘s bestselling series . The plot finds Annabeth Chase (Leah Sava‘ Jeffries) captured by the forces of Kronos, leading Percy (Walker Scobell) to embark on a perilous journey to rescue her. He must free a goddess in chains, confront the Titan’s curse and avoid triggering the fall of Olympus. He’s joined by his friend, the satyr Grover Underwood (Aryan Simhadri), and some unlikely others on his quest. Related Stories Beyond the Book "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return TV E. Lockhart, Gotham Group Tackling Fantasy Novel 'The Curse Workers' for 20th Television (Exclusive) Co-creator/executive producer Jonathan E. Steinberg tells The Hollywood Reporter that Percy and Annabeth’s friendship continues to be central to the story this season. “In the first two seasons, we were very aware that while we were watching a story about two lonely kids become best friends, there were other things in the offing between them, and that eventually, they would mean more to each other,” he says. “Some of that is a romantic story eventually, and some of that is just how best friends they are. Getting to test that and watch them both deal with the idea of losing the other, and maybe never getting them back, is sort of core to the experience of investing in Percy and Annabeth’s relationship.“ Steinberg praises the season‘s handling of the maturity as “exciting.” “Ultimately, it doesn’t matter how tall that monster is, if you don’t care about the two people in the center of the story, it’s just not going to be exciting. This season really answers both of those calls and doing its work on a grand scale and also putting these people through a trial and interrogating how important they really are to each other,” he says. As the third season rolls out, the cast and creatives — including Scobell, Jeffries, Simhadri, Steinberg and EPs Dan Shotz and Craig Silverstein — sat down to talk with THR about the making of the show, bringing the book’s epic moments to life and what fans can expect. Leah Sava’ Jeffries and Walker Scobell in Percy Jackson and the Olympians S eason 3. Disney/Eric Milner Sourcing the Source Material Each season of the show has corresponded with a book in the series. (Season 1 was adapted from 2005’s The Lightning Thief, Season 2 from 2006’s The Sea of Monsters and now Season 3 from 2007’s The Titan’s Curse. ) The books feature monsters and battles and mythical creatures, much of which make for an ambitious adaptation to a TV show. For the producers, their challenge is bringing all of that to life. “Rick doesn’t make it easier for us with each book,” Shotz quips. “It just gets bigger and bigger as we go. But the benefit of doing a series is you get to keep building and learning from what you did before, and have the show grow.” He gives credit to the entire team for “making this the biggest, best version of itself,” including the “massive set pieces.” “You want to deliver on kids’ imaginations and deliver these creatures, but do it unique to Percy,” Shotz adds. “So every time we’re trying to build a creature or create a set piece, it’s like, what makes it unique to this show? How do you take mythology that’s been around for a long time? How do you take what Rick put in his books, and then how do we make it into something that is really special? And it just takes incredible craftsmen and women who just put their best feet forward and deliver on it. The artistry that we got to see this year really felt like it was second to none, and we just went for it.” Scobell in Percy Jackson and the Olympians S eason 3. Disney/David Bukach Silverstein gives credit to Steinberg and Shotz for envisioning something bigger than the small screen. “It starts with the ambition of John and Dan at the outset of this, to say, ‘OK, this isn’t just the TV version. This is the thing ,'” he shares. “We all love big movies. It’s not holding back. These guys really went for it to put this thing up on [a big] scale.” Aryan Simhadri, who plays satyr Grover Underwood, says fans will be pleased this season. “We talk a lot of about the tone shifting, but I’m really proud of how we adapted a lot of the fan-favorite moments from the book,” he says. “I think we really did a good job of visualizing these sets and like adapting these moments to screen. It really just looks stunning this season.” Meanwhile, the actors share that they do a deep dive into the books before filming each season. Asked how much they draw on the source material, Jeffries is quick to reply: “Oh, I drew so much.” Scobell offers his own take. “I feel like it’s really important to start off every season rereading the book that you’re doing,” he says. “I reread Book 3 before we went into it and and I’ve reread Book 2 before we started that [season], and I think that’s really important.But at the same time you have to be willing to kind of let some things go because some things are going to get cut, some things are going to get added. It’s going change the story a little bit, so you kind of have to keep the core of their character but be willing to change according to the script.” Shifting Beyond Percy’s POV One of the challenges for the production team is that that the entire book series is a first-person narrative as told by Percy. “Everything in the book is from Percy’s point of view,” Silverstein says. “We’ve long taken the camera off from around his shoulder, and put it out with other people. It’s kind of been a slowly widening process of that as the story progresses.” But it’s not that easy just to show other characters’ points of view without changing the story. “If the camera cuts to something else that he did not see happen, or someone else he did not see, how does that affect the story of the book?” Silverstein continues. “And in surprising ways, it affects quite a bit. [For example], Percy sees a lot of things through his dreams, but if he doesn’t see those things, then the story’s ahead of him, and sometimes the audience is ahead of him. Sometimes that’s good, and sometimes that’s not good. The challenges to the adaptation begin to present themselves, and then you’re always trying to steer back to what the core of the story is, what made us excited when we read the books, and hoping that that lines up with what made any reader excited when they read the books.” Scobell in Percy Jackson and the Olympians S eason 3. The Annabeth Dilemma Annabeth isn’t in the third book very much, but she’s obviously one of the main characters of the series. For that matter, Clarice (Dior Goodjohn) isn’t in it at all — but she also appears in the third season. So how do you tell a story around characters who have little to no presence in the source material? “It’s about taking cues from the book,” Silverstein says. “Just because Annabeth’s not in the book doesn’t mean she’s not in the story. She is, and it’s about taking the camera to her. We’re trying to build the story out. She’s up there on Mount Othrys with Luke. Well, what are they talking about? What’s going on there? And that’s something that colors within the lines of the grand narrative that doesn’t change it in a huge way.” As for Clarice, she’s not in the book because she’s working on a secret mission for Chiron, but it’s not clear what that mission is to the reader until later. “If you read the later books, you find out what she’s doing,” Silvertein adds. “So [in the series], we’re going to find out what she’s doing a little earlier. Which is what we would have done if we had taken the camera and put it over her shoulder, right? It’s fleshing that stuff out.” The producers do consult with Riordan on these types of changes. According to Shotz, the author loves exploring “all these different avenues” as well. “It gives him an opportunity to dive deeper into this world and make suggestions about what he thinks, is happening, that he didn’t get to explore when he started this process,” Shotz adds. And, of course, Annabeth is crucial to the overall story. “That’s what’s amazing about adaptations is, once you have a character like Annabeth, you can’t keep telling this story without Leah,” Shotz says. “It doesn’t work. We must tell her story, so that’s really the fun part of it, but also for an audience who’s not only going to get their book series honored, but they’re going to get all these new things that will excite them. And that makes it really interesting, so that it’s not just a book report. You’re getting so much more.” Jeffries in Percy Jackson and the Olympians S eason 3. Disney/David Bukach For Jeffries, not having source material to draw on actually allowed a bit more freedom in portraying the character. “I really feel like it was kind of up to interpretation for me because I could do a lot of acting improv, not with words but with reactions and how she plays certain scenes, which is a good thing,” she says. “It’s more of a raw reaction now because when you’re playing a part or you’re doing a certain scene that’s really important in the books, and you know what’s in there, it’s kind of like you expect it. But with Annabeth and with me especially, it was kind of harder I’m also figuring it out. I wanted to make sure that I still stayed in Annabeth’s character, even though she’s not in the book [much].” Still, she admits that she was a bit nervous as a result of not having the anything in the books to draw on. In Season 3, Annabeth also spends much of the story separated from Percy and Grover, which meant Scobell and Simhadri weren’t really there to witness Jeffries acting out her scenes, and vice versa. They were only able to see one another’s performance once the series started coming together, and they have nothing but praise for one another. “Once I watched it and saw everything come together — especially you guys, because I wasn’t with you guys, so I didn’t really get to see what you were doing — you guys looked really good. I’m actually really proud of you guys,” Jeffries says. “it is weird because there were two separate whole stories going on basically at the same time,” Scobell adds. “So, not be there for part of it and then see what’s going on afterward.” “And to see how much you’ve grown at the end of the season,” Simhadri adds of Annabeth. Thalia Joins the Action Thalia, the demigod daughter of Zeus, has been present throughout the books and series but as a tree for much of the story. In the books, the story goes that Zeus did this to protect her after she sacrificed herself to save her friends. But in a twist, the series diverted from the books; viewers learned in the season finale that he actually transformed her as a punishment after she confronted him about his intentions to use her as a weapon. She’s been mentioned through the books and series up to this point, looming large in the characters’ consciousness. We briefly met her in the Season 2 finale after she was transformed back to her human form, but now she’s a much bigger part of the story. This season finds Thalia (Tamara Smart) joining forces with Percy, but it’s a rocky alliance as he is wary of her loyalty to Luke, the demigod who betrayed Percy way back in Season 1 and has been trying to overthrow the Olympian gods. “Rick has a phrase about this book, and it applies to this season as well: All of the major chess pieces are coming onto the board,” Silverstein says. “Thalia has been talked about since Season 1, but now she’s really coming into the story, and when he’s talking about the chessboard, what game is it? Well, it’s this war between the gods and the Titans. And Thalia is right at the center of all of that. Thalia and Percy and any other potential children of the big three gods who may be out there.” Scobell and Tamara Smart in Percy Jackson and the Olympians S eason 3. Disney/David Bukach The overall saga of the books comes more into focus in the third book/Season 3, he adds, versus just focusing on “the quest of the year.” “And what Thalia decides to do will affect not just all of the people she loves and her friends, but the entire world and all of her parents and all of her grandparents,” he adds. “She’s got a big role.” As for how the dynamic changes with Thalia around, the actors say it introduces a rivalry between the characters. Simhadri begins, “We all wanted to be — ” “the biggest and baddest,” Jeffries finishes as he nods. (The cast often finishes each other’s sentences.) Scobell expands: “Thalia is kind of in competition with Percy for his spot in that kind of group. But she can’t just show up and join us. It’s not like [Percy’s cyclops half-brother] Tyson, where he and Grover can exist. There can be only one.” Simhaddri echoes that sentiment: “It’s one or the other.” Art Imitating Life Percy has arguably the biggest growth of any character up to this point, as he started off the series thinking he was a regular boy before learning he was a demigod and becoming a hero. “The most important part about playing Perseus Jackson is also experiencing my own life in the same way,” Scobell says. “He goes to camp every summer and then he goes back to school and back to his real life. I do the same thing. We take a big break in between every season.” But now, Scobell finishing his last year in high school and still awaiting word on a fourth season. “So I’m kind of moving into uncharted territory because before, I could look forward to next season and really just be comfortable going to school and living my own life, but this is going to be a big change for me because it’s so uncertain.” For Simhadri, he also felt like Grover grew a lot of over the course of the season, as did he, not only as a person but as an actor. “I was an adult on season 2, but I never ended up working that many hours per day,” he shares. “But in season 3, I was back every day filming and I was working with a ton of adults, so we would all just shoot for as long as we could in well into the night and really just like push ourselves every day. So I feel like not only did Grover grow over the course of the season, I think I grew in tandem alongside him.” Simhadri in Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3. Disney/David Bukach Why Greek Gods Are Having a Moment This year has seen not only more Percy Jackson but also the box office blockbuster The Odyssey. Why are people suddenly gaga over the Greek gods? “It’s timeless,” Steinberg says. “Those stories have evolved to be about universal experiences that just kind of live really deeply in everybody. I think it’s really not surprising that they never quite go away, because they apply to everybody. We’re happy that it’s in the zeitgeist, but not surprised.” “And Percy did it a lot faster than Odysseus,” Shotz quips of the latter’s 20-year journey back home. *** Percy Jackson and the Olympians is streaming on Disney+ and Hulu. THR

title: Vanessa Ferlito, John Carroll Lynch And Ted Levine Join Denzel Washington In New Thriller From Christopher McQuarrie And United Artists

The film, which is penned by Scott Barkan and Gregg Zehentner, will be released in theaters on October 1. The plot centers on a former police detective serving a life sentence who is diagnosed with terminal brain cancer. Granted compassionate release with six months to live, he returns home to the estranged daughter he left behind and a grandson he never knew existed. He only wants to make amends and forget his dark past, but his dark past has not forgotten him. Related Stories Casting Teyonah Parris To Co-Star With Denzel Washington In Christopher McQuarrie's Thriller For United Artists Casting Denzel Washington And Christopher McQuarrie Team On New Thriller At United Artists And Amazon MGM Studios McQuarrie will also produce alongside Heather McQuarrie along with Stuber and Nick Nesbitt, who produce through United Artists; Joseph Restaino for Hungry Bull Productions; Reza Moheet and Norman Aladjem for Mainstay Entertainment; Katia Washington; and Tommy Harper. Hungry Bull’s Tony Stopperan, Mainstay’s Tim Honigman and Joe Guest will serve as executive producers. Watch on Deadline Ferlito can be seen as a series regular in Chuck Lorre’s series for HBO Max, Bookie , opposite Sebastian Maniscalco. She also appeared in Netflix’s limited series Griselda opposite Sofia Vergara. She recently completed a long-running series regular role on the CBS series NCIS: New Orleans opposite Scott Bakula, and can be seen on the USA Network crime drama Graceland from creator Jeff Eastin. She is represented by Alchemy Entertainment and Innovative Artists. Lynch can currently be seen in the most recent season of Ryan Murphy’s American Horror Story as well as last spring’s The Beauty . He is represented by Suskin/Karshan Management and SRDA. Levine can currently be seen in Netflix’s Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen , created by Haley Z. Boston and executive produced by Matt and Ross Duffer. On television, he recently appeared in Apple TV+’s Cape Fear , executive produced by Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg. He is best known for his eight critically acclaimed seasons on USA Network’s Monk and returned for Peacock’s Mr. Monk’s Last Case: A Monk Movie . title: ‘The Odyssey’ Leads Critics Choice Awards Below-The-Line Shortlists

The Odyssey leads with recognition in 11 of the 12 categories, as designated by a special BTL Nominating Committee — its omission from the best young actor/actress category reflecting the stacked veteran cast which includes Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Jon Bernthal, Tom Holland, Zendaya and Lupita N’yongo, among others. Following The Odyssey are Dune: Part Three and La Bola Negra with eight shortlist placements each, and Godzilla Minus Zero and Wildwood , each with recognition on seven of the shortlists. The ceremony returns to E! for the third consecutive year, and to USA Network for the second, with the telecast airing live on both the East and West coasts from 7:00-10:00 p.m. ET/4:00-7:00 p.m. PT. title: Designing a ‘Hunger Games’ Prequel: From Using 600,000 Flowers in the ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Arena to Recreating the Capitol in the 1970s
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 23, 2026 11:15am PT Designing a ‘Hunger Games’ Prequel: From Using 600,000 Flowers in the ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Arena to Recreating the Capitol in the 1970s By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest Sandra Hüller To Be Honored With Spotlight Award At Palm Springs International Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Ina Garten Says She Turned Down ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Because the Thought of Competing Gave Her ‘Nightmares’ 1 day ago Noah Schnapp Says He Auditioned to Play Haymitch in ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: ‘They Picked Right for This One’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lionsgate Production designer Uli Hanisch thought shooting the highly anticipated “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” in the remote town of Asturias, Spain, meant they would be safe from spoilers. The production would shoot in a desolate valley, requiring an hours-long trek to the set, plus the lack of hotel accommodations and the occasional restaurant nearby, reassured him. Until it happened. “We had the experience from last time where fans were following us to Poland trying to take pictures, but up there, it’s nothing, it’s just us,” Hanisch tells Variety . “We were starting to build up the cornucopia pieces, and I think after two or three days, the first images appeared on the internet. It was somebody saying, ‘Oh, we found them.’ I was like, ‘How is that even possible?’” Related Stories Microdrama Makers From Turkey and Japan Bet on Emotional Hooks and Infuriating Villains at Taiwan Creative Content Fest India's T-Series and Hungama Launch Microdrama Platform FastTV With $32 Million Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) Even though sleuthing fans were able to find it, the location is so secluded that Hanisch wondered if it would be feasible to get a crew of the necessary magnitude all the way up there. But once he saw the luscious greenery contrasting the jagged mountains, he knew they had found the arena for the Second Quarter Quell, and they’d have to make it work. “I stepped out of the car and looked into the valley and said, ‘God damn, yeah, that’s it,’” Hanisch says. “I sent an image to Francis [Lawrence, the franchise’s longtime director], saying, ‘Look, this is our valley, but it’s really far away.’ And he said, ‘Yeah, well, we have to do it here.’” The next step was designing and building the Cornucopia — the focal point of the arena, which distinguishes each iteration of the Hunger Games (and each installment of the film franchise) from the others. Similar to the paradoxical landscape, Hanisch and his team wanted to create something that balanced beauty with danger. They landed on a blossom with metal spikes for petals, surrounded by thick beds of wildflowers, arranged by color, demarking each tribute’s position around the centerpiece. The Cornucopia in “ The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping .” Courtesy of Lionsgate “It’s very beautiful, it’s very elegant, but it also looks very deadly and evil,” Hanisch says. “When they were shooting the opening, and the tributes were all around with these capes, I thought this looked like one of those satanic, strange cults. I thought it was actually a very matching feel.” Once the games begin and the tributes abandon the menacing structure, they are fully immersed in a flourishing woodland environment where the foliage is as deadly as it is extravagant. To bring this to life, Hanisch’s small but mighty team of six worked for three weeks dressing the arena with flowers. The arrangements surrounding the Cornucopia alone required up to 600,000 artificial flowers. “We underestimated it. What you see in the movie is still enhanced by visual effects,” Hansich says. The team also had to invent deceptively beautiful devices like the berms: a mechanical bush that serves as a portal for mutts to enter and exit the arena, and a conduit for Haymitch (Joseph Zada) to destroy it. “Oh, the berms!” Hanisch coos. “The berms were really special because, first of all, what is a berm? We have to come up with some kind of a sensible thing on our own to make it work. It’s hard to tell that as an interesting story because it’s a very long, time-consuming, tiring process.” Concept art from “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” District 12 in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.” Courtesy of Lionsgate While testing the limits of his imagination and portraying the grandeur of the games posed significant production challenges for Hanisch, recreating District 12 was like “coming home.” The cast and crew returned to the same abandoned steel mill factory in Germany where they shot the 2023 prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” and once again captured the dreariness of the downtrodden district. “We agreed that District 12 never changes, which I like very much,” Hanisch says. He may be partial, though, because filming took place near his hometown of Nuremberg. “It’s very beautiful, actually, very intense and complex. I know every corner there.” Recreating Panem’s Capitol didn’t have the fond feeling of going home, but it was familiar and a task that Hanisch holds “close and dear.” With the 2023 prequel “The Battle of Songbirds and Snakes,” the filmmakers decided that the Capitol would be based on Berlin after World War II because “we can see what the situation has done to the city,” Hanisch explains. The timeline for “Sunrise on the Reaping” jumped 20 years into the future, landing in a 1970s aesthetic. “We wanted to explore the capital of Panem at the peak of its power, wealth and arrogance,” he says. So, production returned to the heart of the historic city for its “glorious,” “unique” architecture and its ability to capture the power dynamics they were looking for. “[Berlin’s International Congress Center] looks like a Star Wars spaceship landed in the middle of the city,” Hanisch says. “It’s huge, it has this strange futuristic ’70s approach, it’s abandoned, and we’ve been there before. We were circling around with all our ideas, and then we were like, ‘Oh my God, we have that thing standing there,’ and you realize you can cover a third of the movie and the heart of the capital in this one go.” Scenes from the Capitol in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” filmed in Berlin. Murray Close/Lionsgate Along with the city’s physical assets, emulating the opulence of the ’70s was a choice rooted in the same principle as the arena: that beneath the beauty lies danger. “The ’70s in the Western world are supposed to be in our memory, this progressive time when things started to change with this youth rebellion, but if you look at the ’70s, it was the peak of Western wealth,” Hanisch says. “Besides this angle of the youth rebelling against all of that, the rest of society was extremely saturated. They were proud, untouchable and wealthy in style. That’s why we thought that’s an interesting twist to show. We see something, and we have an idea of what it means, but now all of a sudden it’s the opposite.” The ’70s imagery resulted from Hanisch and the filmmakers’ interpretation of Suzanne Collins’ novel and then Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie’s screenplay. He acknowledges that it is already a challenge to translate books into movies because they are such different art forms, but it’s more difficult, impossible even, to value people’s different interpretations of the material. “Every reader creates their own world while reading it, and you can never say your version is right and your friend’s version is wrong, so we cannot do anything else but what we think is right,” Hanisch says. “It’s more about dealing with the intention of the writer of the novel and then translating it into what you think is right.” This motto keeps Hanisch grounded when dealing with such a massive, devoted fan base: “What more can you do?” “We always think a lot about the fans,” Hanisch says. “I find it so fascinating how important this is for so many people and how seriously they talk and think about it. It’s not really for us. Of course, it’s my job, and I love to do that, and it’s a fantastic thing to be done, but it is mainly to make the fans happy. And they should be happy.” ‘The Nightingale’ Trailer: Dakota and Elle Fanning Share the Screen for the First Time and Play Sisters During WWII in Adaptation of Popular Book Loading comments...

title: Wedding Surprise: Casey Wasserman and Jenny Chandler Reveal Marriage at Friendsgiving-Turned-Reception: “Best. Night. Ever”

The veteran Hollywood mogul, who is steering the ship for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 as chairman, married longtime girlfriend, Jenny Chandler. title: Super Bowl LXI to Touch Down in Imax Theaters
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 23, 2026 11:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A view of Levi's Stadium during the third quarter of Super Bowl LX between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots on February 8, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. Chris Graythen/Getty Images ESPN, Walt Disney and the National Football League have agreed a first-time deal to see Super Bowl LXI broadcast live on the big screen in Imax theaters in the U.S. and select international markets. With Super Bowl LXI the first for ESPN in the sport media brand’s history, its four-hour game day telecast on Feb. 14, 2027 will feature the main championship game telecast, the halftime show headlined by Jay-Z and pregame and postgame coverage. The Imax partnership is part of an effort by Walt Disney to make the 2027 Super Bowl telecast as widely accessible as possible. “Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and Imax takes it to a historic new scale,” Ken Potrock, president, major event integration for The Walt Disney Company, said in a statement on Monday. “With ESPN’s first Super Bowl, we’re reaching fans across an unprecedented range of platforms and meeting them wherever they want to be, with unique moments that only Disney and ESPN can deliver,” he added. Walt Disney plans to leverage every part of its portfolio, from theme parks to films to products and experiences to drive awareness to the 2027 Super Bowl game. In an era of 70-inch TV screens and sporting events in sports bar, the NFL is also looking to bring its game day live event product to even bigger screens, with food and beverages on sale in the lobby. The NFL in 2017 struck a sponsorship deal with Canadian cinema giant Cineplex to show Sunday Night Football and the Super Bowl broadcast live on its movie screens north of the U.S. border. And Cinemark recently unveiled plans to bring a Monday Night Football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Seattle Seahawks on Dec. 7 to a first-ever in-market NFL watch party at its theater in West Plano, Texas, as part of another sponsorship deal. NFL games are currently shown in COSM venues as well. “The Super Bowl is a one-of-a-kind global cultural event imbued with spectacle, sound, drama, and heroes — all the makings of a great Imax experience,” Rich Gelfond, CEO of Imax said in his own statement. “This is a milestone for Imax that further elevates our standing as a premier global platform for entertainment and events, and we’re excited to work in partnership with Disney, ESPN and the NFL to give football fans an unforgettable night.” The Super Bowl LXI game telecast promises to be the largest live event ever for Imax as its large format theaters in Australia, New Zealand and Brazil will also broadcast the championship NFL game. As the NFL looks to broaden its international audience, including on more digital platforms, ESPN earlier announced additional content like Super Bowl LXI with Peyton and Eli (ESPN2), Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show (ESPNU), Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats (NFL Network), and the first-ever Star Wars Funday Football animated telecast on Disney+, Disney Channel and Disney XD. ESPN’s Monday Night Football broadcast team of Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge will call the Super Bowl LXI game. THR

Animated features can also compete in other categories, best picture included, and a country’s official international feature submission can be considered for animated feature. On the documentary side, the 190 films cover just about everything: music, politics, art, sports and true crime. The contenders include “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie,” “Ask E. Jean,” “Marc by Sofia,” “Avedon,” “Lorne,” “Musk,” “The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist,” “EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert,” “Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It,” “Man on the Run,” “Free Leonard Peltier,” “The Trial of Alec Baldwin” and “My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile.” One of the biggest titles that pundits will be keeping their eyes on is Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “ You Can See Everything ,” the A24 cultural sensation that just surpassed $100 million globally , a rare box office milestone for a documentary. Some docs also still need to finish their qualifying runs. Films that won a qualifying festival award or were submitted as a country’s official international feature selection are eligible as well, and that crossover is all over this year’s lists. Fourteen titles show up in both races, among them Palestine’s “Citizen Osama,” the United Kingdom’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” Ukraine’s “Traces,” Iceland’s “The Ground beneath Our Feet,” Switzerland’s “Who Is Still Alive” and Albania’s “State Film.” The Documentary branch picks both the shortlist of 15 and the eventual five nominees. In international feature, 100 of the 104 films were submitted by countries or regions. The other four got in through the Academy’s festival award pathway: Berlin Golden Bear winner “Yellow Letters,” Sundance World Cinema Grand Jury Prize (Dramatic) winner “Shame and Money,” Busan Award for best film winner “Midday Meal” and Toronto Platform Award winner “Angh.” The Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” was also the official selection of Romania. Official submissions include France’s “Minotaur,” Spain’s “ La Bola Negra ,” Brazil’s “Gugu’s World,” Norway’s “Growth of the Soil,” Germany’s “Everytime,” Italy’s “The Spiral,” Japan’s “All of a Sudden,” South Korea’s “Possible Love,” Mexico’s “On the Road,” Denmark’s “Woman Unknown,” Iran’s “Land of Angels,” India’s “Gondhal” and Canada’s “Nina Roza.” To qualify, an international feature must run longer than 40 minutes, be produced outside the United States and have dialogue that’s more than 50% non-English. Members from every branch can opt in to the preliminary round if they meet the minimum viewing requirement. That shortlist also lands Dec. 15. Preliminary voting for select categories runs Monday, Dec. 7, through Friday, Dec. 11. Shortlists follow Tuesday, Dec. 15, and nominations will be announced Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars take place Sunday, March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood. The ceremony airs live on ABC, streams live on Hulu and reaches more than 200 territories worldwide. The partners plan to present it across hundreds of Imax locations in the U.S. and select international markets including Australia, New Zealand and Brazil. It will mark Imax’s largest live event. The specific theater count hasn’t yet been finalized. “Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and IMAX takes it to a historic new scale,” said Ken Potrock, Disney’s President, Major Event Integration. Watch on Deadline “The Super Bowl is a one-of-a-kind global cultural event imbued with spectacle, sound, drama, and heroes — all the makings of a great IMAX experience,” said Rich Gelfond, CEO of the big screen exhibitor, calling it a milestone for the company. Potrock noted that Super Bowl LXI is “reaching fans across an unprecedented range of platforms and meeting them wherever they want to be,” with Imax adding the communal experience of movie theaters to ESPN, ABC, Disney+ and Univision. In fact, the wide availability of the top-rated telecast has irked local ABC affiliates even before this latest partnership. With Disney+ and ESPN’s streaming service carrying the game, along with numerous alternative telecasts on ESPN, the core ABC broadcast risks getting overshadowed, as the stations see it. The one-day only event will begin at 6 pm ET and feature ESPN’s main Super Bowl LXI game, the Apple Music Halftime Show headlined by Jay-Z, and pregame and postgame coverage in a presentation of more than four hours. ESPN’s Monday Night Football broadcast team of Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge will call the game. ESPN’s presentation plans for the game include previously announced viewing options including Super Bowl LXI with Peyton and Eli (ESPN2), Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show (ESPNU), Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats (NFL Network), and the first-ever Star Wars Funday Football animated telecast (Disney+, ESPN App, Disney Channel and Disney XD). A promotional spot and materials supporting the theatrical event will start to roll out this week. Tickets are expected to go on sale in January 2027. title: Why New Wave Music Won’t Go Away: New Documentary Explores How Synthesizers, MTV and Androgyny Built the Enduring Genre
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 23, 2026 10:25am PT Why New Wave Music Won’t Go Away: New Documentary Explores How Synthesizers, MTV and Androgyny Built the Enduring Genre By Pat Saperstein Plus Icon Pat Saperstein Deputy Editor @Variety_PatS Latest Why New Wave Music Won’t Go Away: New Documentary Explores How Synthesizers, MTV and Androgyny Built the Enduring Genre 3 hours ago Hello Sunshine’s Lauren Neustadter to Leave Reese Witherspoon’s Company at End of Year 3 days ago ‘I Play Rocky’ Fact vs Fiction: Butkus the Dog, Bloody Knuckles and Stallone’s Fight to Get ‘Rocky’ Made 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mike Prior / Koh Hasebe/Shinko Music / Lynn Goldsmith From “Stranger Things” to virtually any Trader Joe’s, new wave music is inescapable. Not only are bands like B-52s , Duran Duran, Tears for Fears and Billy Idol still frequently touring, new generations are embracing the danceable sounds of 1977 to 1987, whether the tunes are making shoppers dance at your local Trader Joe’s or soundtracking a nostalgia-tinged TV series. How has the genre managed to hang on for so long, even as rock is no longer the dominant sound across the music scene? The new docuseries “New Wave,” premiering Monday on MGM+, tells the story of how a loosely connected group of misfits, fashionistas and punk rockers from the U.K. and U.S. coalesced to form a movement — and how the dawn of music videos then propelled that music into the stratosphere. Related Stories Microdrama Makers From Turkey and Japan Bet on Emotional Hooks and Infuriating Villains at Taiwan Creative Content Fest India's T-Series and Hungama Launch Microdrama Platform FastTV With $32 Million Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) In the doc, musicians, DJs and veejays (Martha Quinn! Mark Goodman!) consider the ingredients that created the movement: the influence of women, the colorful and original fashions of the era and the dawn of MTV, all coming together to create a joyful decade of energetic music that still resonates today. Interviews in the four-part series include Kate Pierson and Fred Schneider of the B52s, Billy Idol, Mark Mothersbaugh of Devo, Danny Elfman of Oingo Boingo, Stewart Copeland of the Police, John Taylor of Duran Duran, Curt Smith of Tears for Fears, Johnny Marr of the Smiths, Kathy Valentine of the Go-Gos, Brian Setzer of Stray Cats and Jim Kerr of Simple Minds. New wave torchbearer Richard Blade, the KROQ and Sirius First Wave DJ who has helped keep fans engaged with the sound ever since it started, serves as consulting producer, with Douglas Tirola directing. R.J. Cutler and Elise Pearlstein are among the executive producers. The production company is This Machine Filmworks, a part of Sony Pictures Television. Speaking with Variety , the B52s’ Pierson and the creative team broke down how new wave got started and labeled, how the series was put together and why the music has endured so long. Why did you think new wave needed its own documentary series? Douglas Tirola: The idea was that by telling this story, we would sort of defend new wave. I think a lot of people think of it as a keyboard, two people, a synthesizer, and a band from Britain making quirky dance music. It’s so much more than that. New wave brought the alternative into the mainstream. It changed music, movies, TV, design, fashion, politics, and how we look at and go out with one another. Everybody loves the music of their youth; it’s their soundtrack, and it’s nostalgic to them. I felt there was a belief system behind new wave, and that’s what the story set out to show. Elise Pearlstein: New wave was a short period — really only about 10 years — but so much music was created and the culture changed during that time. There had never really been a documentary that looked specifically at new wave, so we all thought it was high time. The term new wave in regards to music is often credited to Sire Records founder Seymour Stein. Why did it need its own term, and what did the bands have in common? Pearlstein: It was really a marketing term. New wave artists were originally grouped with punk, and punk wasn’t commercial. Some venues didn’t want punk acts to play because they would destroy the place. So “new wave” was a marketing term created to distinguish new wave artists from the punk movement and, ultimately, make them more commercially viable. And it worked. Kate Pierson: I really think it’s a made-up term trying to encompass post-punk. Punk was just evolving; this was a sort of evolution from punk. The whole idea was that you could express yourself in any way, and anyone could do it. I think the thing about new wave that changed from punk was that it was inclusive. There were a lot more women, queer artists and Black artists in the scene. Having a mixed band, with queer men and women in it, made us very different and unique in that scene. But it really fit into the whole new-wave fashion: it was fashion-forward and had eclectic influences. There was also technology — the addition of synthesizers and electronic music. Every band was so different from the others. New wave embraced all these different styles: danceable music, funky music, even some disco influences. We loved disco. Doug, your previous project was about Leonard Bernstein, from a much earlier time. Why did this era lend itself much more to making a very visual documentary? Tirola: There were more people running around with video cameras, even if they were big. With the explosion of cable, more people were producing content, even if it was cable access. That was a relief. Once you hit the ’80s, there’s a lot more out there. R.J. Cutler: It coincides with the arrival of MTV, which was a great gift to the filmmakers. Pearlstein: A lot of the bands came from art school. Talking Heads and the B-52s were interested in visual media and the visual medium, so they embraced visual storytelling around music. Even before making music videos, bands like Devo were playing around with film and visuals in their music. How did new wave influence style at the time? Pierson: The ripped garbage-bag look that Belinda Carlisle wore, or Debbie Harry’s style — it was this fusion of punk, avant-garde style and thrift-store chic. It was very “anything goes” and experimental fashion, which was so great. I think we (the B-52s) made an impact visually, so MTV embraced us, and that helped a lot. How did you come up with the throughline of the series, which tells the story of the rise and fall and rise of new wave? Pearlstein: Because it’s a pretty tight chronology — it’s only a 10-year period — we looked at the arc of new wave. It went from obscurity to a pretty fast demise within that time. We looked at how it broke out and became mainstream, how it peaked and jumped the shark, and then how it dissipated. We also looked at milestones, like the synthesizer, which democratized the ability to make this kind of music, and MTV. Bob Geldof’s Band Aid and Live Aid were important moments when everybody came together, and you saw the diversity of the music as well as its commitment to change. Then new wave started showing up in ads and getting co-opted by the mainstream. Ultimately, it was parodied. Once it got too extreme, some artists, like U2, didn’t want to be associated with new wave; they wanted to be beyond a genre. Cutler: The fundamental story of outsiders becoming insiders is a great landscape for dramatic storytelling. Tirola: Richard Blade was an absolute resource throughout this entire thing. He helped us get some of the interviews, gave us information, and gave us some of the key plot points. One point was when new wave took off. Richard talked about three songs that came out in a short period of time. One was Gary Numan’s “Cars.” I’d never put those three songs together that way before. New wave took the place of disco. Then, when some things didn’t work out, the industry said, “No, we don’t want New Wave,” and then it had a comeback. What were some of your favorite interviews in the series? Tirola: I thought John Taylor was incredible. He said during the interview, “Thank God someone’s finally making this.” (Kate Pierson) also understood what new wave was: it was for outsiders, but outsiders who wanted to be in the mainstream. Every interview was great, but that one was special. Billy Idol, who I was a fan of but had never met, was so insightful and detail-oriented. He understood the bigger idea we were going for: where new wave fits into the big picture. Bono of U2 performs at the US Festival, a major California event which helped bring new wave music into the mainstream. Redferns Who would you have liked to get but weren’t able to? Tirola: U2 comes to mind. I feel like Bono and their early story would have been interesting. I think people forget they weren’t always a stadium band. Richard Blade: When U2 played at the US Festival, they were a small band. If you look at the running order, they opened for Missing Persons. Bono went to climb the speaker stacks and wave his rebel flag, as he liked to do at concerts, and security grabbed his leg and pulled him down: “What do you think you’re doing? Get down from there!” Back then, he was just this scruffy little Irish guy trying to climb the speaker stacks. It’s amazing to see them go from that to perhaps the biggest rock band in the world You still hear new wave music everywhere, especially in movies and TV shows. How has it managed to endure so long? Are younger people embracing new wave? Blade: The younger generation is growing up with it now because it’s been used so many times in commercials. If you watch an NFL game, every third commercial — if it’s not Peyton Manning selling something — has an ’80s song playing. “Stranger Things” was the perfect example of that, and so many shows followed its influence on the ’80s. It’s not just the parents, and it’s not going to fade away as we get older. People will continue to love Depeche Mode, The Cure and Duran Duran, just as people love the Beatles, The Who, The Beach Boys and The Rolling Stones. Pearlstein: The B-52s really epitomize that (staying power). The music is fun, danceable, hopeful, sticky, addictive — and it makes you feel good. I also think 20-somethings today have rediscovered New Wave in a huge way. The gender fluidity new wave embraced is back today, and the sounds, looks, and goth style are all popular again. Cutler: It captures the spirit of youth forever. For those of us whose youth it’s tied to, it’s always resonant, but there’s also a timelessness to its spirit of rebellion and inclusion. The combination makes it forever young, and that’s really exciting. It’s still driving culture. title: Taylor Swift, a Brenda Lee Superfan, Presents the Star With 10x Platinum Plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 23, 2026 10:22am PT Taylor Swift, a Brenda Lee Superfan, Presents the Star With 10x Platinum Plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’ By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Taylor Swift, a Brenda Lee Superfan, Presents the Star With 10x Platinum Plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’ 2 hours ago Ateez Debuts at No. 1 on Billboard 200 for the Third Time This Year; U2’s ‘Carnaval de Luz’ Bows at No. 4 21 hours ago Noah Kahan Deserved a Lot More Grammy Love Than Just One Minor Nomination. Here’s Why He Didn’t Get It 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source TAS Rights Management Taylor Swift has gone on record from early in her teens forward as a Brenda Lee fan, and on her recent trip to Nashville she got to honor her predecessor in country-pop crossover stardom with a plaque honoring the diamond-selling status of Lee’s “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.” Only two Christmas singles have been certified by the RIAA for selling 10 million copies, with Lee’s 1958 signature smash becoming the second, following Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” A video posted on Instagram and X shows Swift knocking on the door to a room where the 81-year-old Lee is awaiting a visitor. “No way,” Lee says, upon first being greeted. “You grow a foot?” Swift responds, “One per year, yeah.” Got the biggest surprise ever to kick off this Rockin' season! @TaylorSwift surprised me in Nashville with a @RIAA Diamond plaque commemorating 10 million copies of "Rockin' Around The Christmas Tree". Only the second Christmas song in history to reach this milestone! 🎄 pic.twitter.com/Nl1K65EbSe — Brenda Lee (@BrendaLeeMusic_) November 23, 2026 Getting to the matter at hand, Swift says, “ I’m one of the many, many fans of your iconic song ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.’ It is such an incredible song. And I’m not the only person who feels that way, because I’m very honored to get to present you with your diamond certification for more than 10 million copies. You recorded this when you were only 13 years old, and it is one of only two Christmas songs to ever reach this milestone. You’re in very good company with Mariah Carey, all the way at the top, and this is yours now, and it will be yours forever… On behalf of all the fans and all the families and people whose Christmases this song has absolutely added dazzle and sparkle and warmth to, thank you so much for your incredible work.” Lee immediately thinks of collaborators who are not around to join the celebration. “Well, the writer, Johnny Marks, who’s no longer here, would be so proud. And all the musicians and (producer) Owen Bradley, everybody, all the fans…” “I’m so happy to get to have this moment with you,” Swift says, noting she has “been such a fan for so long.” “And I’m a fan,” responds Lee. “Oh, really?” “Yes. I wish you wasn’t so tall,” says Lee, who at the so-called height of her fame, when she was known as “Little Miss Dynamite,” stood at 4 feet 9 inches. They join the previously announced returning star and producer Camila Mendes, Leslie Bibb, and Marisa Tomei. The Gulfstream Pictures and Honor Role film is currently in production in Italy, with Becca Gleason directing. Plot details for Upgraded 2 are under wraps. Amazon MGM Studios has the worldwide distribution rights for the sequel, penned by returning screenwriters Luke Roberts and Justin Matthews. Set in both London and New York City, the rom-com chronicles the trials and tribulations of balancing work, romance, and following your dreams. Previously, she was in Mark Mylod’s The Menu with Anya Taylor-Joy and Ralph Fiennes. Carrero is represented by 3 Arts Entertainment, Gersh, and Skrzyniarz & Mallean. Matthews is known for her work in Disney’s Frozen II , Universal’s Happy Death Day and Happy Death Day 2U , Lionsgate’s The Duel , CW’s Batwoman , Hulu’s Looking for Alaska , and Netflix’s Do Revenge . She also executive produced Upgraded through Honor Role, a film and television production company launched in 2024 with Mendes. Schulz recently completed his global Life Tour, which culminated in his 2025 Netflix special, Life . He most recently starred in Paramount and Legendary Pictures’ live-action adaptation of Street Fighter , and will next star in Universal Studios’ Miami Vice ’85, as well as Apple Original Films’ Running. Schulz is represented by CAA, manager Dov Mamann, and Yorn Levine. Jackson’s TV credits include Channel 4’s hit sitcom Derry Girls, BBC’s Liverpool-set gangster drama This City Is Ours, Netflix’s period comedy series The Decameron and Lisa McGee’s How To Get To Heaven From Belfast . title: Steven Spielberg To Helm ‘Heart In Winter’ With Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy & Mark Rylance; Paul Thomas Anderson Scripting For Focus
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Steven Spielberg To Helm ‘Heart In Winter’ With Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy & Mark Rylance; Paul Thomas Anderson Scripting For Focus Read the full story By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin ‘Shōgun’ Star Hiroyuki Sanada Joins Destin Daniel Cretton’s ‘Naruto’ At Lionsgate Steven Spielberg Sets Adaptation Of ‘The Heart In Winter’ As Next Film At Focus With Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy And Mark Rylance Starring And Paul Thomas Anderson Adapting The Script Bruce Greenwood, Johnny Knoxville And Dylan Hawco Join ‘Fake Skating’ Adaptation At Sony View All November 23, 2026 9:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Steven Spielberg, Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy, Paul Thomas Anderson And Mark Rylance /Getty//Getty/Getty EXCLUSIVE: For years, Steven Spielberg has talked about how much he’s wanted to direct a Western and it now looks like the three-time Oscar winner has found the perfect project to saddle up for. Sources tell Deadline, Spielberg is developing an untitled film for Focus Features and has assembled an all-star roster of A-list talent to bring it together. Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy and Mark Rylance are set to star in the film, directed by Spielberg from a script by Oscar winner Paul Thomas Anderson , based on Kevin Barry’s The Heart in Winter . The film will come out some time in 2028 and follows two star-crossed fugitives trying to find a place for themselves in the American West. Kristie Macosko Krieger, Sara Murphy, Anderson and Spielberg will produce the film. Tim Headington, Neil Shah, Ryan Zacarias, and Ana Leocha will executive produce. Related Stories News Indie Holiday Push: 'Minotaur', 'Elsinore' & 'Josephine' Debut With Cameron Winter Concert Film; 'Club Kid' Expands - Specialty Preview News Danny Boyle Talks 'Ink', The Common Architecture Of His Movies And More '28 Years Later' As He Receives The Deadline Legend Award Spielberg spoke with Deadline about his decision to make this his first Western, and said not only did the story speak to him, but the opportunity to work with his longtime friend Anderson was too good to pass up. Watch on Deadline “It’s really the excitement for me to get to work together with my dear friend and colleague Paul Thomas Anderson on a genre, but more particularly, the genre notwithstanding, a story that quite quickly became close to both our hearts and we felt that we could do as a team.” This will mark the first time Anderson has written something without directing it too, which just shows how much the Oscar-winning director wanted to work with Spielberg. Though many view Anderson more for his directing then writing, he is coming off an Oscar win for best adapted screenplay for One Battle After Another, a novel many believed was too tough of a story to adapt. Spielberg said the two had begun talking about potentially working together since January and while they hadn’t on this book since then, they very much wanted to make something set in America in the late 1800s. “We’ve sat in screening rooms, and by the way, only on 35mm film, and watched dozens of Westerns,” Spielberg added. As for the casting process, Spielberg said they were his top choices, and frankly Buckley and Murphy were “the only two actors that could play these characters.” “This story is about the people who refused to settle for a life that is less then they deserve but maybe more than they can handle,” Spielberg said. “Jessie and Cillian were the first people to ever come to mind for this and they also have never made a film together.” Spielberg was also super excited at the idea of making the film at Focus Features after working with the studio on Hamnet, which he produced, and would land Buckley an Oscar for Best Actress at the 2026 Oscars. “I’m really excited to be working with Kujo at Focus after doing Hamnet together, so it’s a reunion in a sense for Jessie and it’s also a reunion for PTA who did Phantom Thread at Focus Features,” Spielberg said. “It’s going to be a real hybrid production with Universal handling production, who will release through the Focus label, and both teams are going to work very closely with each other, which I’m very excited for as I know both worlds at Universal intimately.” Spielberg has a longstanding relationship with Universal Pictures and Focus Features. Most recently, Spielberg released Disclosure Day with Universal Pictures, which opened at No. 1 at the box office to critical acclaim. Spielberg also recently produced Hamnet for Focus Features, which received eight Oscar nominations, with Buckley winning Best Actress. Spielberg added that his selections for below the line are still in process, but the plan is to shoot next year in the winter. As for the question of whether this film was also a metaphor for his directing riding off into the sunset and making it his last film, not only is it not, but the iconic director has an idea of how he would want to do that when that day comes. “If I wanted to ride off into the sunset, I would have done Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade next and I could have had those characters literally riding off into the sunset as the credits roll,” Spielberg said. Besides Hamnet, Buckley can be seen next in Three Incestuous Sisters, which also stars Saoirse Ronan, Dakota Johnson and Josh O’Connor. Murphy can be seen next in the new prison drama from Damien Chazelle that also stars Daniel Craig and Michelle Williams. Buckley is represented by CAA, United Agents and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. Murphy is represented by WME and Sloane Offer Weber & Dern. Rylance is represented by CAA and Peikoff Mahan Law Office.
